# Installation

Whisker apps are regular Rust crates driven by the `whisker` CLI. This
page sets up the toolchain; the next page scaffolds and runs an app.

## Prerequisites

- **Rust 1.85 or newer** (install via [rustup](https://rustup.rs)).
- **iOS**: Xcode and its Command Line Tools. Simulator builds work out
  of the box.
- **Android**: an Android SDK, an NDK (`27.1.12297006` recommended; 23.1
  through 27.1 are supported), and JDK 17 or newer. Installing Android Studio
  covers all three: Whisker finds its SDK at `~/Library/Android/sdk` and its
  bundled JDK without `ANDROID_HOME` or `JAVA_HOME`.
- **Web**: the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` Rust target and a modern browser.
- **Desktop**: the native build toolchain for your OS and graphics drivers
  supported by wgpu. `whisker run desktop` currently ships the macOS path.

Add the device build targets you plan to use:

```bash
rustup target add aarch64-apple-ios-sim    # iOS Simulator (Apple silicon)
rustup target add aarch64-linux-android    # Android device/emulator
rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown   # Web
```

On an Intel Mac, the iOS Simulator needs `x86_64-apple-ios` instead of
`aarch64-apple-ios-sim`. `whisker run ios` builds only the Simulator slice
your Mac runs natively.

## Install the CLI

```bash
cargo install whisker-cli
```

This installs the `whisker` command (and a `cargo whisker` alias). It is the
user-facing entry point for every Host. Xcode and Gradle can also invoke
Whisker's build adapter from their own build phases, so generated mobile
projects remain buildable from the native IDEs.

## Check your setup

`whisker doctor` inspects your toolchain and reports exactly what's
present or missing — Rust targets (iOS, Android, and Web), the Android
SDK, NDK, `adb`, and JDK, and Xcode. It looks for the SDK and JDK the same
way builds do, so a passing doctor means the build can find them:

```bash
whisker doctor
```

Fix anything it flags before moving on. You can scope it with
`--no-ios` or `--no-android` if you only care about one platform. See
the [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference.md) for all options.

## Next

Continue to [Your First App](/docs/your-first-app.md) to scaffold and run a
project.

# Your First App

With the [toolchain installed](/docs/installation.md), you're three commands
from a running app.

## Scaffold

```bash
whisker new my-app
cd my-app
```

This generates a single-crate project that compiles standalone:

```text
my-app/
├── Cargo.toml          # crate + whisker dependency
├── src/lib.rs          # your app — a #[whisker::main] function
├── whisker.rs          # app config (bundle id, name, platform settings)
├── rust-analyzer.toml
├── .gitignore
└── README.md
```

The generated `src/lib.rs` is a working counter, split into small
components. Styles are trimmed here:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

#[whisker::main]
fn app() -> Element {
    render! { Root }
}

/// The full-screen background. It holds no state.
#[component]
fn root() -> Element {
    render! {
        View(style: css!(flex_grow: 1.0 /* … */)) {
            Counter
        }
    }
}

/// Owns the count and hands it to `Card`.
#[component]
fn counter() -> Element {
    let count = signal(0);
    render! { Card(count: count) }
}

/// The UI you see on screen — the part you edit.
#[component]
fn card(count: RwSignal<i32>) -> Element {
    render! {
        View(style: css!(/* … */)) {
            Text(value: "My App")
            Text(value: "Tap +1, then edit `Card` and save. The count survives hot reload.")
            Text(value: computed(move || format!("{}", count.get())))
            View(style: css!(/* … */)) {
                Button(label: "-1", delta: -1, count: count)
                Button(label: "+1", delta: 1, count: count)
            }
        }
    }
}

#[component]
fn button(label: &'static str, delta: i32, count: RwSignal<i32>) -> Element {
    render! {
        View(on_tap: move |_| count.set(count.get() + delta), style: css!(/* … */)) {
            Text(value: label)
        }
    }
}
```

## Run

Choose a Host. Boot a simulator/emulator first when using mobile:

```bash
whisker run ios
whisker run android
whisker run web
whisker run desktop
```

The first run sets up the native host project under `gen/`, builds your
crate, and installs and launches the app. It takes a moment; subsequent
runs are much faster.

> **Targets are positional**: `whisker run ios` / `whisker run android` /
> `whisker run web` / `whisker run desktop`
> (not `--ios`). See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference.md) for flags
> like `--bind` and `--no-tui`.

## Edit with hot reload

Leave `whisker run` running. Tap **+1** a few times, then edit `Card` in
`src/lib.rs` — change the title, tweak a style, add a `View`. Save, and the
change **hot reloads** onto the running app in about a second. The count
keeps its value: only `Card` is rebuilt, and the count lives in `Counter`.

Hot reload rebuilds the components you edited from scratch, so state owned
by an edited component resets. Keep state in a component above the ones you
iterate on, as the template does. Editing `Root`, `app()`, or code outside
components (a helper function, a type) rebuilds the whole UI. See
[Hot Reload](/docs/hot-reload.md) for the details.

Changes to `whisker.rs` (bundle id, app name, platform settings) reshape
the native project, so they need a full `whisker run` restart rather than
a hot reload.

## Next

- [Project Structure](/docs/project-structure.md) — what each file does.
- [Components & `render!`](/docs/components.md) — start building real UI.

# Project Structure

A Whisker app is an ordinary Rust crate with one Whisker configuration file.

```text
my-app/
├── Cargo.toml      # crate manifest + `whisker` dependency
├── src/lib.rs      # the app: a #[whisker::main] function
├── whisker.rs      # app configuration (compiled separately by the CLI)
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
├── gen/            # generated Host projects (do not edit, gitignored)
└── target/         # cargo build output (gitignored)
```

## `src/lib.rs`

Your application. It contains exactly one
[`#[whisker::main]`](/docs/macros.md) function returning an
[`Element`](/docs/elements.md), plus any
[`#[component]`](/docs/components.md) functions you add. As your app grows,
split it across modules and additional crates like any Rust project.

## `whisker.rs`

App **configuration** — bundle id, display name, version, and per-platform
settings. Its `main` function uses `whisker_cng::run`:

```rust
fn main() {
    whisker_cng::run(|app| {
        app.name("My App")
            .bundle_id("com.example.myapp")
            .version("1.0.0");
    });
}
```

`whisker.rs` generates platform projects when executed. `whisker run` and
`whisker build` compile it separately from `src/lib.rs` and execute the same
generation entry point before building the app. This is also
where you register [plugins](/docs/modules-and-plugins.md). Full field list:
[Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-api.md).

## `gen/`

Generated **Host projects**. Depending on the command, CNG materializes a
Gradle project under `gen/android/`, an Xcode project under `gen/ios/`, a
Cargo-based native project under `gen/macos/`, or a WASM/browser shell under
`gen/web/`. `whisker run` and `whisker build` share this tree, so:

- **Don't edit it by hand** — changes are overwritten. Shape the native
  side through `whisker.rs` and [plugins](/docs/plugin-api.md) instead.
- **Don't commit it** — it's in `.gitignore`. Delete it any time for a
  clean regenerate.

## `Cargo.toml`

A normal crate manifest. It depends on `whisker` and `whisker-cng` (with default
features disabled), and registers `whisker.rs` as a binary requiring the `whisker-config` feature. This
lets rust-analyzer provide completion without extra editor configuration and
keeps the configuration binary and its generation engine out of default builds. See
[Cargo registration](/docs/app-configuration.md#cargo-registration-and-editor-support).

Add
[first-party modules](/docs/modules-api.md) (like `whisker-router` or
`whisker-image`) here as you need them.

## Next

- [Editor Setup](/docs/editor-setup.md) — get autocompletion working.
- [Components & `render!`](/docs/components.md) — build your UI.

# Editor Setup

Whisker is plain Rust, so any editor with
[rust-analyzer](https://rust-analyzer.github.io/) gives you
autocompletion, go-to-definition, and inline type errors out of the box —
VS Code, Zed, JetBrains (RustRover/IntelliJ with the Rust plugin), Neovim,
and others.

## Recommended setup

1. Install **rust-analyzer** for your editor.
2. Open the project root (the folder with `Cargo.toml`).
3. Let it index once; after that, completion and diagnostics are live.

## Completion inside `render!`

`render!` is a macro, but it's written so rust-analyzer can still help
inside it:

- Element names complete (`Vie` → `View`, `Te` → `Text`).
- Keyword-argument names complete (`View(sty…` → `style`).
- Component names and their props complete like any function call.

If completion inside the macro ever looks stale, a quick "restart
rust-analyzer" / reload refreshes its macro expansion.

## Formatting

Use [`whisker fmt`](/docs/formatting.md) — a rustfmt drop-in that formats your
Rust _and_ the `render!` / `css!` macro bodies (and the expressions inside
them) that plain `cargo fmt` leaves untouched. It respects your
`rustfmt.toml` and nothing else.

For format-on-save, point rust-analyzer at its `--stdin` mode in a
`rust-analyzer.toml` at the project root:

```toml
[rustfmt]
overrideCommand = ["whisker", "fmt", "--stdin"]
```

`whisker new` scaffolds this file automatically, so new projects get
`render!`/`css!` format-on-save out of the box. See
[Formatting](/docs/formatting.md) for the full setup.

## Next

You're set up — head to [Components & `render!`](/docs/components.md) to
start building, or browse the [API Reference](/docs/overview.md).

# Components & `render!`

A Whisker UI declaration builds a tree of small [`Element`](/docs/elements.md)
handles. Built-in elements and user components both expose ordinary Rust
builders; `render!` adds named-argument and nested-body syntax on top.

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

render! {
    View(style: css!(padding: px(16))) {
        Text(value: "Hello, Whisker")
        View(on_tap: move |_| println!("tapped")) {
            Text(value: "Tap me")
        }
    }
}
```

The same tree can be built without the macro:

```rust
View::builder()
    .style(css!(padding: px(16)))
    .body(|body| {
        body.push(Text::builder().value("Hello, Whisker").build());
    })
    .build()
```

`render!` does not special-case `View`, `Text`, or your component names. Every
node follows the same `Type::builder().prop(value).body(...).build()` contract.

## Syntax

- Named arguments go in parentheses: `View(style: style, on_tap: handler)`.
- Children go in a trailing body: `View { Text(value: "hi") }`.
- Parentheses are optional when there are no named arguments.
- A Rust expression child is written as `{expression}`; an iterable can be
  spread with `..items`.
- Text literals and primitive values can be children where text content is
  accepted. `Text(value: ...)` is the explicit text element form.

Use [`whisker fmt`](/docs/formatting.md) to format composition bodies. Plain
`rustfmt` deliberately leaves macro contents untouched.

## App entry point

Each app has one `#[whisker::main]` function. Keep it small and mount a root
component. Hot reload rebuilds only the components you edit, and editing
`app()` or the root component rebuilds the whole UI, so keep state in
components below the root and above the ones you iterate on:

```rust
#[whisker::main]
fn app() -> Element {
    render! { Root }
}

#[component]
fn root() -> Element {
    render! { View { Text(value: "It works") } }
}
```

## Defining components

Annotate an idiomatic `snake_case` function with `#[component]`. The macro
generates a PascalCase marker, a props type, and a public builder:

```rust
#[component]
fn greeting(name: Signal<String>, excited: Option<bool>) -> Element {
    let suffix = if excited.unwrap_or(false) { "!" } else { "" };
    render! { Text(value: computed(move || format!("Hello, {}{suffix}", name.get()))) }
}

render! {
    Greeting(name: "world", excited: true)
}
```

`Greeting(...)` lowers to `Greeting::builder()...build()`. Required props are
tracked in the builder type state, so omitting `name` is a compile-time error.
`Option<T>`, `Children`, and props with `#[prop(default = ...)]` may be omitted.
Required and optional props may appear in any order.

The component function runs when it mounts. Signals and computed properties
then update their exact renderer bindings; Whisker does not repeatedly diff a
virtual tree. A hot-reload patch remounts a component when its source changes,
which resets that component's own signals; other components keep their state.
See [Hot Reload](/docs/hot-reload.md).

## Static and reactive props

A prop typed `Signal<T>` accepts either a plain `T` or a signal handle:

```rust
let count = signal(0);

render! {
    Badge(label: "items") // static
    Counter(value: count) // reactive
}
```

Inside the component, `value.get()` participates in dependency tracking. If a
built-in builder receives a signal directly, it installs the effect needed to
reapply that property. Passing `count.get()` instead passes a one-time snapshot.

## Defaults and children

```rust
#[component]
fn card(
    #[prop(default = px(16))] padding: Length,
    children: Children,
) -> Element {
    render! {
        View(style: css!(padding: padding)) {
            {children()}
        }
    }
}

render! {
    Card {
        Text(value: "Inside the card")
    }
}
```

A `children: Children` parameter adds the builder's trailing `body` method.
`Children` is reusable, so framework-level components can project it more than
once, although ordinary layout components usually call it once.

## Moving a prop into a closure

Hot reload can run a component's body again, so the body may borrow its props
but never give one away. Moving a non-`Copy` prop such as `id: String` straight
into a `move` closure fails with `E0507: cannot move out of value, a captured
variable in an FnMut closure`. Clone it into a local first and move the local:

```rust
#[component]
fn row(id: String) -> Element {
    // effect(move || println!("showing {id}")); // E0507
    let row_id = id.clone();
    effect(move || println!("showing {row_id}"));
    render! { Text(value: id.clone()) }
}
```

`Copy` props, including every `Signal<T>` and signal handle, move freely.

## What's next

- [Styling](/docs/styling.md)
- [State Management](/docs/state-management.md)
- [Lists & Conditionals](/docs/lists-and-conditionals.md)
- [Macro Reference](/docs/macros.md)

# Styling

Every visual element accepts one structured `style` value. Whisker does not
parse CSS strings at runtime: property names and values are Rust methods and
types, so unsupported combinations fail during compilation.

```rust
use whisker::css::{AlignItems, Color, Display, FlexDirection};
use whisker::prelude::*;

render! {
    View(style: css!(
        display: Display::Flex,
        flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column,
        align_items: AlignItems::Center,
        gap: px(12),
        padding: px(16),
        border_radius: px(12),
        background_color: Color::hex(0x1A1A2E),
    )) {
        Text(value: "Card", style: css!(color: Color::hex(0xFFFFFF)))
    }
}
```

## `css!` and `Css`

`css!` is named-argument syntax over the public `Css` builder. These forms are
equivalent:

```rust
let a = css!(padding: px(16), opacity: 0.8);

let b = Css::builder()
    .padding(px(16))
    .opacity(0.8);
```

Use the macro for declarations embedded in UI and the builder when ordinary
Rust composition, generics, or conditional method calls are clearer. `Css`
values are owned, cloneable declaration sets and can be returned from helper
functions or merged before use.

Raw strings are intentionally rejected:

```text
View(style: "padding: 16px") // does not compile
```

## Values and units

Length helpers make units explicit:

```rust
px(16)
percent(100)
1.25.rem()
24.rpx()
90.deg()
250.ms()
```

Keyword values use enums such as `Display::Grid`,
`JustifyContent::SpaceBetween`, or `Overflow::Hidden`. Colors, gradients,
transforms, shadows, clip paths, transitions, and animations use structured
value or shorthand builders rather than encoded strings.

## Layout

Whisker resolves structured declarations in Rust and sends computed layout
inputs to Taffy. The supported layout surface follows Taffy's capabilities:

- block, flexbox, and grid layout;
- absolute and relative positioning;
- intrinsic measurement for text and Host elements;
- percentages, min/max constraints, aspect ratio, gaps, and overflow clipping.

The Host receives final logical-pixel geometry. Browser or native layout is not
the source of truth, so the same tree uses the same layout model on every Host.

## Paint and platform coverage

The Rust frame protocol represents semantic paint such as backgrounds, borders,
rounded corners, shadows, transforms, opacity, clipping, text, and image
resources. Each Host implements those operations with its platform renderer.
Properties outside layout generally follow Whisker's supported Lynx-compatible
subset, excluding removed vendor-only features. The
[CSS Reference](/docs/css.md) lists the actual typed surface; a method's presence
on `Css` is the compile-time contract.

## Reactive styles

Pass a `ReadSignal<Css>` or `RwSignal<Css>` directly to `style` to reapply it
when dependencies change:

```rust
let selected = signal(false);
let card_style = computed(move || {
    Css::builder()
        .padding(px(16))
        .background_color(if selected.get() {
            Color::hex(0x2563EB)
        } else {
            Color::hex(0x1F2937)
        })
});

render! {
    View(
        style: card_style,
        on_tap: move |_| selected.set(!selected.get()),
    ) {
        Text(value: "Select")
    }
}
```

Passing a computed style keeps the declaration reactive. Passing
`card_style.get()` takes a snapshot, just like other signal-backed props.

## Reuse and custom properties

Ordinary Rust functions and constants are the simplest reuse mechanism:

```rust
fn card_style() -> Css {
    css!(padding: px(16), border_radius: px(12))
}
```

Typed custom properties are also available when a value must inherit through
the element tree or participate in a reusable style fragment. They retain CSS
`var(--name, fallback)` semantics while values remain structured; Whisker does
not expose a selector cascade or stylesheet class system.

# State Management

A Whisker component function runs **once**, when it mounts. There is no
re-render of the whole function when state changes. So how does the UI
update? Through **signals**: reactive values that remember who reads
them and notify exactly those readers when they change.

This is the single idea to internalize:

> **Reading a signal inside a View(or an effect/computed) subscribes
> that one spot to the signal. Writing the signal re-runs only the spots
> that read it** — a text node, a style attribute, a derived value — and
> nothing else.

No virtual DOM, no diffing, no component re-execution. Just targeted
updates at the precise places that depend on the value.

## Creating state

Make a signal with `signal(v)`. It hands back a single read/write handle
— an `RwSignal<T>` — that both reads and writes the same slot:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let count = signal(0);
count.get();               // 0  — read
count.set(7);              // replace
count.update(|n| *n += 1); // mutate in place → 8
```

`signal(initial)` returns `RwSignal<T>`. `RwSignal::new(initial)` is the
equivalent explicit constructor — `signal(0)` is just the idiomatic
shorthand:

```rust
let count = signal(0);        // idiomatic
let count = RwSignal::new(0); // identical
```

The handle is `Copy`, so it moves into `move |_|` closures freely —
copying a handle does **not** clone the underlying value; both copies
point at the same slot.

You **read** with `.get()` (returns a clone, subscribes the current
tracking context) or `.with(|v| …)` (borrows the value, no `Clone`
bound). You **write** with `.set(v)` (replace) or `.update(|v| …)`
(mutate in place — what you want for collections like
`update(|v| v.push(item))` and for types that aren't `Clone`).

`set` and `update` notify every reader even when the new value equals the old
one. Readers behind a [`computed`](#deriving-values-with-computed) are spared,
because a computed notifies only when its result changes. When a write may
repeat the current value and something expensive reads the signal directly,
compare first:

```rust
if count.get_untracked() != next {
    count.set(next);
}
```

There is **no call sugar**: a signal is read and written through these
methods, never by calling it. Write `count.get()` and `count.set(1)`,
not `count()` or `count(1)`. Full method tables live in the
[Reactivity reference](/docs/reactivity-api.md).

## The one rule, made concrete

Here is the whole model in one example:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let count = signal(0);

render! {
    View {
        // `count.get()` reads the signal here, so this text node
        // subscribes. When count changes, ONLY this text updates.
        Text(value: computed(move || format!("Count: {}", count.get())))

        View(on_tap: move |_| count.update(|n| *n += 1)) {
            Text(value: "+1")
        }
    }
}
```

Tapping `+1` runs the handler, which mutates `count`. The runtime then
re-runs only the text interpolation that read `count` — not the whole
component, not the sibling views. That is fine-grained reactivity.

## Deriving values with `computed`

When you need a value that depends on other state, don't recompute it by
hand — derive it with `computed`. The closure re-runs whenever a signal
it reads changes, and the result is cached:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let count = signal(0);
let label = computed(move || format!("You clicked {} times", count.get()));

render! {
    Text(value: label)   // updates whenever count changes
}
```

`computed(f)` returns a `ReadSignal<T>` — the _same_ type a plain signal
hands out — so you read it with `.get()` just like any other signal, and
you can pass it anywhere a reactive value is accepted.

Computed values are **memoized**: subscribers are only notified when the
new result actually differs from the previous one (`T: PartialEq`). A
computed whose inputs change but whose output stays the same costs
nothing downstream. See
[`computed`](/docs/reactivity-api.md#computed) for details.

## How signals flow into `render!`

This is the most important everyday rule, and it's visible right at the
call site:

- **Pass a signal handle → reactive.** The attribute or prop tracks the
  signal and updates live.
- **Pass `.get()` or a plain value → a static snapshot.** The value is
  read once, at the call site, and never updates.

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let name = signal("world".to_string());

render! {
    Text(value: name)        // reactive — re-renders when `name` changes
    Text(value: name.get())  // snapshot — captures the value once
    Text(value: "literal")   // static — never changes
}
```

The same rule applies to your own `#[component]` props. A prop typed
`Signal<T>` accepts _either_ a plain value or a signal handle, and
chooses static-vs-reactive based on what you pass. This is
[The Signal prop type](/docs/reactivity-api.md#the-signal-prop-type), and
it's why `Badge(label: "items")` and `Badge(label: my_signal)` are both
valid calls to the same component.

## A worked example: counter with a derived label

Putting it together — a counter, a derived parity label, and a button:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

#[component]
fn counter() -> Element {
    let count = signal(0);
    let parity = computed(move || {
        if count.get() % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }
    });

    render! {
        View {
            Text(value: computed(move || {
                format!("Count: {} ({})", count.get(), parity.get())
            }))
            View(on_tap: move |_| count.update(|n| *n += 1)) {
                Text(value: "Increment")
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`count` is the source of truth. `parity` derives from it and only
notifies its reader when the even/odd result flips. The button's handler
is the only writer. Three independent reactive spots, one signal — no
manual wiring.

## Splitting read/write

An `RwSignal` carries both capabilities, but you don't always want to
hand both to everyone. When you pass state into a child component, you
usually want to grant exactly one capability — a child that _displays_
state shouldn't be able to _mutate_ it, and vice versa. The `RwSignal`
projects into narrower handles:

- **`count.read_only()` → `ReadSignal<T>`** — a read-only view of the
  same slot. Pass this to a child that should only display the value.
- **`count.write_only()` → `WriteSignal<T>`** — a write-only handle. Pass
  this to a child whose only job is to mutate.
- **`count.split()` → `(ReadSignal<T>, WriteSignal<T>)`** — both halves at
  once, the Solid-style pair. Handy when one site reads and a different
  site writes.

All three project onto the **same underlying slot** — they don't copy the
value — and like `RwSignal` they're `Copy`, so they move into closures
freely.

The recommended pattern for sharing state with a child is to keep the
`RwSignal` in the parent and pass down the narrowest handle the child
needs:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

#[component]
fn parent() -> Element {
    let count = signal(0);
    render! {
        View {
            // `Display` only reads → hand it a read-only handle.
            Display(count: count.read_only())
            // `Controls` both reads and writes → hand it the RwSignal.
            Controls(count: count)
        }
    }
}
```

If you prefer the explicit pair up front, destructure with `.split()`:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let (count, set_count) = signal(0).split();
count.get();               // ReadSignal — read only
set_count.set(7);          // WriteSignal — write only
set_count.update(|n| *n += 1);
```

This is the only place you'll see the `(read, write)` tuple form — it's a
deliberate split, not the default way to create a signal.

## When state must outlive its owner: `Arc*` signals

Arena signals (`RwSignal`, `ReadSignal`, `WriteSignal`) are tied to the
[owner](/docs/reactivity.md#ownership-and-cleanup) that created them and are
freed automatically when that component unmounts. That's the right
default.

When a signal must **outlive** its declaring scope — process-global
state in a `static`/`OnceLock`, state shared across independently-mounted
screens, or a `HashMap<K, ArcRwSignal<V>>` — reach for the
reference-counted `Arc*` family instead. They stay alive as long as any
handle remains, and they mirror the arena types' method shape (they're
`Clone` rather than `Copy`). See
[Arc signals](/docs/reactivity-api.md#arc-signals--arc_signal--the-arc-family).

Converting an Arc signal into an arena handle (`let s: RwSignal<T> =
arc.into()`) ties the new handle to the owner running at that moment. The Arc
keeps the value alive, but that particular handle is freed with its owner, and
reading it afterwards panics. Keep the `ArcRwSignal` itself in the `static` or
map, and convert inside the component that reads it.

## Non-reactive storage: `StoredValue`

Not everything needs to be reactive. If you want owner-scoped storage
that's freed on unmount but does **not** subscribe on read or notify on
write — the scoped equivalent of `Rc<RefCell<…>>` — use
[`StoredValue`](/docs/reactivity-api.md#storedvaluet):

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

let history = StoredValue::new(Vec::<String>::new());
history.update(|h| h.push("event".to_string()));
```

And if a value is decided once at mount and never changes, skip signals
entirely and use a plain Rust binding — there's no reason to pay for
reactive bookkeeping a constant doesn't need.

983	## Effects: reacting to change
984	
985	A `computed` derives a _value_. An `effect` runs a _side effect_ — the
986	bridge from reactive state to the outside world: logging, persistence,
987	animation, syncing to a native API.
988	
989	```rust
990	use whisker::prelude::*;
991	
992	let count = signal(0);
993	
994	effect(move || {
995	    log::info!("count is now {}", count.get());

997	```
998	
999	An effect runs **once immediately** when created (this first run is
1000	synchronous — it has executed by the time `effect` returns), recording
1001	every signal it reads. From then on it re-runs whenever any of those
1002	signals changes:
1003	
1004	```rust
1005	let count = signal(0);
1006	
1007	effect(move || log::info!("count = {}", count.get()));
1008	// ^ logs "count = 0" right away
1009	
1010	count.set(5);   // schedules the effect; it logs "count = 5"
1011	count.set(8);   // logs "count = 8"
1012	```

1031	## Tracked vs untracked reads
1032	
1033	By default, reading a signal inside an effect or computed **subscribes**
1034	to it. Sometimes you want to read a value _without_ making it a
1035	dependency — say, to read configuration once inside an effect that
1036	should only re-run for some other reason. That's what the `_untracked`
1037	variants are for:
1038	
1039	```rust
1040	use whisker::prelude::*;
1041	
1042	effect(move || {
1043	    let tracked = position.get();            // re-runs when position changes
1044	    let snapshot = config.get_untracked();   // read, but does NOT subscribe
1045	    renderer::draw(tracked, snapshot);
1046	});
1047	```
1048	
1049	The pairs are:
1050	
1051	- `get` / `get_untracked` — clone-read the value.
1052	- `with` / `with_untracked` — borrow the value (`|v: &T| -> R`), avoiding
1053	  a clone for expensive or non-`Clone` types.
1054	
1055	Use the tracked forms (`get` / `with`) for inputs the effect should react
1056	to; reach for `_untracked` only when subscribing would cause an unwanted
1057	re-run. Over-subscribing is the more common mistake, so the untracked
1058	variants are a deliberate, occasional tool.

1060	## Batching: one update wave per handler
1061	
1062	Writing a signal does **not** run its subscribers synchronously. Writes
1063	enqueue their subscribers, and the queue is drained at a flush boundary —
1064	typically the end of an event handler. This means multiple writes in one
1065	handler produce a **single** update wave:
1066	
1067	```rust
1068	use whisker::prelude::*;
1069	
1070	View(on_tap: move |_| {
1071	    set_first.set("Ada".to_string());
1072	    set_last.set("Lovelace".to_string());
1073	    set_dirty.set(true);
1074	    // ↑ an effect (or computed, or {expr}) that reads two or three of
1075	    //   these runs exactly ONCE here, when the handler returns — not
1076	    //   once per write.
1077	}) {
1078	    Text(value: "Update")
1079	}
1080	```
1081	
1082	This is the Solid/Leptos "microtask batching" model. You almost never
1083	have to think about it — it just means there's no glitchy intermediate
1084	state and no redundant work. In tests or a custom driver you can force

1088	## Ownership and cleanup
1089	
1090	Every `#[component]` runs inside a fresh **reactive scope**, called an
1091	`Owner`. Every signal, computed, effect, and lifecycle hook you create in
1092	the component body belongs to that scope. When the scope is **disposed**,
1093	all of them are torn down together:
1094	
1095	- the signals it allocated are freed,
1096	- its effects and computeds stop running,
1097	- and its cleanup callbacks fire.
1098	
1099	This is what makes Whisker leak-free without manual unsubscription: state
1100	lives exactly as long as the component that owns it.
1101	
1102	### `on_mount` and `on_cleanup`
1103	
1104	Two hooks bracket a component's life in the tree:
1105	
1106	```rust
1107	use whisker::prelude::*;
1108	
1109	#[component]
1110	fn timer() -> Element {
1111	    let elapsed = signal(0);
1112	
1113	    on_mount(move || {
1114	        log::info!("Timer is now on screen");
1115	        // good place to start work that needs the view to exist
1116	    });
1117	
1118	    on_cleanup(move || {
1119	        log::info!("Timer is being removed");
1120	        // release resources, cancel subscriptions, etc.
1121	    });
1122	
1123	    render! {
1124	        Text(value: computed(move || format!("Elapsed: {}", elapsed.get())))
1125	    }
1126	}
1127	```
1128	
1129	- `on_mount(f)` fires once, **after** the component's view has been
1130	  attached to the tree — the right place for post-mount measurement or
1131	  kicking off background work.
1132	- `on_cleanup(f)` fires when the owning scope is disposed. Multiple
1133	  registrations run in **LIFO** order (last-registered, first to run),
1134	  which lets later setup tear itself down before earlier setup.

1136	### When does disposal happen?
1137	
1138	A component's scope is disposed when it's removed from the tree. The most
1139	common triggers are the reactive control-flow primitives:
1140	
1141	- When a [`Show`](/docs/lists-and-conditionals.md) condition flips, the
1142	  branch that's no longer active has its scope disposed — its signals,
1143	  effects, and `on_cleanup` callbacks all run.
1144	- When an item drops out of a [`ForEach`](/docs/lists-and-conditionals.md)
1145	  (its key disappears), that item's scope is disposed. Items whose keys
1146	  survive keep their scope — and their local state — intact across
1147	  re-renders.
1148	
1149	```rust
1150	use whisker::prelude::*;
1151	
1152	let show_panel = signal(true);
1153	
1154	render! {
1155	    Show(when: move || show_panel.get(), fallback: || render! { Fragment() }) {
1156	        // Signals and effects created in here are disposed the moment
1157	        // `show_panel` becomes false, and recreated fresh if it flips back.
1158	        ExpensivePanel()
1159	    }
1160	}
1161	```

1164	"set up a subscription in `on_mount`, tear it down in `on_cleanup`" is a

1194	## Conditional rendering with `Show`
1195	
1196	`Show` mounts its children while the `when` predicate reads `true`, and an
1197	optional `fallback` while it reads `false`. The predicate is a reactive
1198	closure — `move || …` that reads a signal — so the branch flips
1199	automatically when that signal changes:
1200	
1201	```rust
1202	use whisker::prelude::*;
1203	
1204	#[component]
1205	fn greeting() -> Element {
1206	    let signed_in = signal(false);
1207	
1208	    render! {
1209	        View(style: css!(display: Display::Flex, flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column, gap: 8.px())) {
1210	            View(on_tap: move |_| signed_in.set(!signed_in.get())) {
1211	                Text(value: "toggle")
1212	            }
1213	            Show(
1214	                when: move || signed_in.get(),
1215	                fallback: move || render! { Text(value: "Please sign in") },
1216	            ) {
1217	                Text(value: "Welcome back!")
1218	            }
1219	        }
1220	    }
1221	}
1222	```
1223	
1224	When omitted, `fallback` renders nothing. On every flip the old branch is
1225	fully disposed before the new one mounts, so reactive state from the hidden
1226	branch can't leak.

1228	## Keyed lists with `ForEach`
1229	
1230	`ForEach` renders one element per item in a `Vec`. It takes three props:
1231	
1232	- `each` — a reactive `move || Vec<T>` items source,
1233	- `key` — `|item: &T| -> K` deriving a stable key, and
1234	- `children` — `|item: T| -> Element` rendering one row.
1235	
1236	```rust
1237	use whisker::prelude::*;
1238	
1239	#[derive(Clone)]
1240	struct Todo { id: u32, title: String }
1241	
1242	#[component]
1243	fn todo_list(todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>) -> Element {
1244	    render! {
1245	        View(style: css!(display: Display::Flex, flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column, gap: 4.px())) {
1246	            ForEach(
1247	                each: move || todos.get(),
1248	                key: |todo: &Todo| todo.id,
1249	                children: |todo: Todo| render! {
1250	                    Text(value: todo.title)
1251	                },
1252	            )
1253	        }
1254	    }
1255	}
1256	```

1258	### Why keys matter
1259	
1260	`ForEach` diffs the new list against the previous frame **by key**, not by
1261	position. That's what lets it tell that an item moved, was inserted, or was
1262	removed:
1263	
1264	- a **kept** key reuses the existing element and its per-item state, so
1265	  anything reactive inside a row survives a reorder;
1266	- a **new** key creates a fresh row;
1267	- a **missing** key disposes that row.
1268	
1269	So the key must be stable and unique per item — a database id is ideal.
1270	Using the list index as a key defeats this: when the list reorders, state
1271	ends up attached to the wrong item.

1273	## When to reach for `list` instead

1275	`ForEach` materializes **every** item into the tree, which is fine for
1276	short lists. For large or scrolling collections, use the virtualized

1278	they scroll into view. Its shape mirrors `ForEach`, except identity
1279	and the per-item layout metadata travel together through a `meta`
1280	prop:
1281	
1282	```rust

1284	    each: move || posts.get(),
1285	    meta: |p: &Post| ItemMeta::key(p.id.clone())
1286	        .reuse_identifier("post")
1287	        .estimated_size(120),
1288	    children: |p: Post| render! { post_row(post: p) },

1295	headers, multi-column `waterfall`, snap paging).

1297	## Combining them: a list with an empty state
1298	
1299	`Show` and `ForEach` compose. Here a `Show` renders an empty-state message
1300	when the list is empty, and the `ForEach` renders the rows otherwise:
1301	
1302	```rust
1303	use whisker::prelude::*;
1304	
1305	#[derive(Clone)]
1306	struct Todo { id: u32, title: String }
1307	
1308	#[component]
1309	fn todos(todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>) -> Element {
1310	    render! {
1311	        View(style: css!(display: Display::Flex, flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column, gap: 4.px())) {
1312	            Show(
1313	                when: move || todos.get().is_empty(),
1314	            ) {
1315	                Text(value: "Nothing to do yet")
1316	            }
1317	            ForEach(
1318	                each: move || todos.get(),
1319	                key: |t: &Todo| t.id,
1320	                children: |t: Todo| render! { Text(value: t.title) },
1321	            )
1322	        }
1323	    }
1324	}
1325	```
1326	
1327	Run it with `whisker run ios`.

1336	# Handling Events
1337	
1338	Event handlers are builder arguments. They run on the `RuntimeInstance` while
1339	the Host is driving an input transaction, so they can update signals directly:
1340	
1341	```rust
1342	use whisker::prelude::*;
1343	
1344	#[whisker::component]
1345	fn Counter() -> Element {
1346	    let count = signal(0);
1347	
1348	    render! {
1349	        View(on_tap: move |_| count.update(|value| *value += 1)) {
1350	            Text(value: computed(move || format!("Count: {}", count.get())))
1351	        }
1352	    }
1353	}
1354	```
1355	
1356	## Pointer handlers
1357	
1358	`View`, `Text`, `ScrollView`, and module elements share the `ElementBuilder`
1359	pointer methods:
1360	
1361	- `on_tap`, `on_click`
1362	- `on_touchstart`, `on_touchmove`, `on_touchend`, `on_touchcancel`
1363	- the corresponding `_catch`, `on_capture_*`, and
1364	  `on_capture_*_catch` variants
1365	
1366	The normal handler participates in the bubble phase. Capture handlers run from
1367	the root toward the target. A `catch` handler stops propagation at that
1368	listener. Hit testing and propagation happen in Whisker's retained scene, so
1369	the semantics do not change between Hosts.
1370	
1371	```rust
1372	View(on_capture_tap: |_| println!("outer capture")) {
1373	    View(on_tap_catch: |event| {
1374	        println!("tap at {}, {}", event.detail.x, event.detail.y);
1375	    }) {
1376	        Text(value: "Tap")
1377	    }
1378	}
1379	```
1380	
1381	## Event metadata
1382	
1383	`TouchEvent` includes surface coordinates, pointer identity/type, buttons,
1384	active touches, and both `target` and `current_target`. An element's `id` and
1385	structured `Dataset` are included in those targets.
1386	
1387	```rust
1388	View(
1389	    id: "album",
1390	    dataset: Dataset::new().int("album_id", 42),
1391	    on_tap: |event| {
1392	        if let Some(value) = event.target.dataset.get("album_id") {
1393	            println!("album: {value:?}");
1394	        }
1395	    },
1396	)
1397	```
1398	
1399	## Scroll and animation events
1400	
1401	`ScrollView` and `List` expose `on_scroll: Fn(ScrollEvent)`. Its detail contains
1402	the current offset, content and viewport sizes, deltas, and drag state.
1403	
1404	CSS transitions and keyframe animations expose lifecycle handlers such as
1405	`on_animationstart`, `on_animationend`, `on_animationcancel`,
1406	`on_transitionstart`, and `on_transitionend`.
1407	
1408	## Module events
1409	
1410	A `#[whisker::module_element]` event prop is deserialized from
1411	`WhiskerValue` into the Rust event type declared in the function signature.
1412	Function-shaped modules use `PlatformModule::on_event`; keep the returned
1413	subscription alive for as long as events are needed.
1414	
1415	See the [event type reference](/docs/events.md) for exact payload fields.
1416	
1417	# Context
1418	
1419	Some values are needed all over the tree: the current theme, the
1420	logged-in user, an app-wide store, the router's navigation stack.
1421	Threading those through every component as props — _prop drilling_ —
1422	gets tedious fast, and every intermediate component has to forward a prop
1423	it doesn't even use. **Context** lets an ancestor publish a value that any
1424	descendant can read directly.
1425	
1426	## Providing and consuming
1427	
1428	Call `provide_context(value)` in an ancestor to make a value available to
1429	everything below it. A descendant reads it with `use_context::<T>()`,
1430	which returns the nearest provided value of that type:
1431	
1432	```rust
1433	use whisker::prelude::*;
1434	
1435	#[derive(Clone)]
1436	struct Theme {
1437	    dark: bool,
1438	}
1439	
1440	#[whisker::main]
1441	fn app() -> Element {
1442	    // Publish at the root...
1443	    provide_context(Theme { dark: true });
1444	
1445	    render! {
1446	        View {
1447	            Toolbar()
1448	        }
1449	    }
1450	}
1451	
1452	#[component]
1453	fn toolbar() -> Element {
1454	    // ...read it anywhere below, no props in between.
1455	    let theme = use_context::<Theme>().expect("Theme provided at root");
1456	    let bg = if theme.dark {
1457	        Color::hex(0x111111)
1458	    } else {
1459	        Color::hex(0xFFFFFF)
1460	    };
1461	
1462	    render! {
1463	        View(style: css!(background_color: bg)) {
1464	            Text(value: "Toolbar")
1465	        }
1466	    }
1467	}
1468	```
1469	
1470	`use_context::<T>()` returns `Option<T>` — it's `Some` when an ancestor
1471	provided a `T`, and `None` otherwise. Provide above, and the lookup is
1472	`Some`; the `.expect(...)` above documents the invariant and turns a
1473	missing provider into a clear message.
1474	
1475	## Borrowing without cloning
1476	
1477	`use_context::<T>()` hands back a **clone** (so `T: Clone`). When `T` is
1478	expensive to clone — or you only need to peek — use `with_context`, which
1479	borrows the value for the duration of a closure:
1480	
1481	```rust
1482	let is_dark = with_context::<Theme, _>(|t| t.dark); // Option<bool>
1483	```
1484	
1485	`with_context::<T, _>(|v| ...)` returns `Option<R>` — `Some(result)` when
1486	a `T` is in scope, `None` when it isn't.
1487	
1488	## Context is keyed by type
1489	
1490	A context is stored and looked up by its Rust type `T`. That has two
1491	practical consequences.
1492	
1493	First, **define a newtype per concern** rather than reusing a bare
1494	primitive. Providing a `String` and later providing another `String`
1495	would collide; wrapping each in its own struct keeps them distinct:
1496	
1497	```rust
1498	#[derive(Clone)]
1499	struct CurrentUser(String);
1500	
1501	#[derive(Clone)]
1502	struct ApiBaseUrl(String);
1503	
1504	provide_context(CurrentUser("ada".into()));
1505	provide_context(ApiBaseUrl("https://api.example.com".into()));
1506	```
1507	
1508	Second, a closer descendant can **shadow** an ancestor's value by
1509	providing the same type again. Lookups walk up from where you are and
1510	stop at the nearest provider, so a subtree can override the theme (or any
1511	context) just for itself:
1512	
1513	```rust
1514	#[component]
1515	fn dark_section() -> Element {
1516	    provide_context(Theme { dark: true }); // overrides the ancestor here down
1517	
1518	    render! {
1519	        View { /* ...descendants see the dark theme... */ }
1520	    }
1521	}
1522	```
1523	
1524	## When to reach for it
1525	
1526	Context fits app-wide, cross-cutting state: a theme, the current user, a
1527	shared store, a router's back-stack. It's the same mechanism Whisker's
1528	own [Routing](/docs/routing-api.md) uses under the hood to expose the
1529	navigation stack to your screens.
1530	
1531	For the full signatures — including how context relates to the reactive
1532	owner tree — see the [Reactivity reference](/docs/reactivity-api.md#context).
1533	
1534	# Async & Data Loading
1535	
1536	Whisker supplies a small task bridge rather than choosing an application-wide
1537	async runtime or HTTP client. The Host continues to own its event loop, and a
1538	`RuntimeInstance` advances local futures during short drive transactions.
1539	
1540	## Local async work
1541	
1542	Use `spawn_local` when a future can run on the current runtime thread:
1543	
1544	```rust
1545	let state = signal(ResourceState::Loading);
1546	
1547	spawn_local(async move {
1548	    match load_profile().await {
1549	        Ok(profile) => state.set(ResourceState::Ready(profile)),
1550	        Err(error) => state.set(ResourceState::Error(error.to_string())),
1551	    }
1552	});
1553	```
1554	
1555	The future may be non-`Send`. Because it resumes inside the same
1556	`RuntimeInstance`, it can update that instance's signals directly.
1557	
1558	## Blocking and CPU-heavy work
1559	
1560	Do not perform a blocking HTTP request, filesystem operation, image decode, or
1561	large parse directly in an event handler. The runtime is executing on the Host
1562	UI thread during that callback.
1563	
1564	```rust
1565	let stories = signal(Vec::<Story>::new());
1566	let error = signal(None::<String>);
1567	
1568	spawn_local(async move {
1569	    let result = run_blocking(move || {
1570	        let body = ureq::get("https://example.com/stories.json")
1571	            .call()
1572	            .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?
1573	            .into_string()
1574	            .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?;
1575	        parse_stories(&body)
1576	    })
1577	    .await;
1578	
1579	    match result {
1580	        Ok(value) => stories.set(value),
1581	        Err(message) => error.set(Some(message)),
1582	    }
1583	});
1584	```
1585	
1586	`run_blocking` sends the closure to a worker thread and resolves the result back
1587	on Whisker's local executor. The closure and return value must be `Send +
1588	'static`.
1589	
1590	The HTTP library in this example is intentionally not part of Whisker. Choose a
1591	transport that supports your target set; a native blocking client does not
1592	automatically work in WebAssembly.
1593	
1594	## Resources
1595	
1596	`resource` packages loading, ready, and error state behind reactive accessors:
1597	
1598	```rust
1599	let stories = resource(|| async {
1600	    run_blocking(fetch_and_parse_stories).await
1601	});
1602	
1603	render! {
1604	    View(style: css!(flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column)) {
1605	        Show(when: move || stories.loading()) {
1606	            Text(value: "Loading…")
1607	        }
1608	        ForEach(
1609	            each: move || stories.get().unwrap_or_default(),
1610	            key: |story| story.id,
1611	            children: |story| render! { Text(value: story.title) },
1612	        )
1613	    }
1614	}
1615	```
1616	
1617	Choose `resource_sync` when the producer is synchronous but you still want the
1618	same reactive state model.
1619	
1620	## Callbacks from another thread
1621	
1622	For callback-based libraries, capture the current instance's dispatcher before
1623	leaving the runtime thread:
1624	
1625	```rust
1626	let dispatcher = runtime_dispatcher().expect("inside Whisker runtime");
1627	
1628	start_operation(move |value| {
1629	    dispatcher.post(move || result.set(value));
1630	});
1631	```
1632	
1633	The dispatcher wakes the correct Host/runtime pair and rejects work after that
1634	instance shuts down. This matters when an application contains multiple
1635	`WhiskerView` instances.
1636	
1637	See [Tasks & Threading](/docs/tasks.md) for exact API constraints.
1638	
1639	# Imperative Handles
1640	
1641	Persistent UI state should remain declarative. A small set of actions instead
1642	target an already-mounted Host element: scroll now, focus now, or send a
1643	module-specific command. Handles provide that escape hatch without exposing a
1644	Host object to application code.
1645	
1646	```rust
1647	use whisker::prelude::*;
1648	
1649	#[whisker::component]
1650	fn Page() -> Element {
1651	    let scroller = ScrollViewHandle::new();
1652	
1653	    render! {
1654	        View(on_tap: move |_| scroller.scroll_to(0.0, true)) {
1655	            Text(value: "Top")
1656	        }
1657	        ScrollView(element_ref: scroller.r()) {
1658	            // long content
1659	        }
1660	    }
1661	}
1662	```
1663	
1664	The handle becomes bound when the element mounts and is cleared when it
1665	unmounts. It can be copied into multiple closures. Built-in typed handles hide
1666	the raw command name and payload.
1667	
1668	Module authors can wrap `ElementRef::command(name, WhiskerValue)` in their own
1669	typed handle. Commands are ordered, one-way operations in the frame protocol;
1670	use a platform module function when the caller needs a return value.
1671	
1672	See [Imperative Handles](/docs/refs.md) for the built-in handle list and error
1673	semantics.
1674	
1675	# Modules & Plugins
1676	
1677	Whisker keeps the rendering kernel small and has two extension points with
1678	different responsibilities.
1679	
1680	## Modules extend the running application
1681	
1682	A **Whisker module** contributes either or both of:
1683	
1684	- a Host element, such as a text input, map, video surface, or native toggle;
1685	- a function-shaped Host service, such as storage, haptics, or system status.
1686	
1687	The Rust crate owns the typed public API and an element schema. Android, iOS,
1688	Web, and desktop each own an independently compiled Host implementation. The
1689	sides match stable module, element, property, event, and command names at
1690	runtime. This loose baseline means native IDE builds do not depend on generating
1691	Swift or Kotlin contracts from Rust source.
1692	
1693	Every value crossing a module boundary is `WhiskerValue`. Built-in `View` and
1694	`Text` use the same element registry and frame protocol as third-party Host
1695	elements; the core does not give custom elements a second-class path.
1696	
1697	## Plugins extend project generation
1698	
1699	A **plugin** changes the CNG project model before `gen/` is written. It can add
1700	permissions, dependencies, manifest/plist values, files, or native build
1701	settings. Plugins do not run inside the application and should not be used for
1702	runtime calls.
1703	
1704	| Need                                  | Use                                   |
1705	| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
1706	| Render a native control               | module element                        |
1707	| Call a platform service               | module function                       |
1708	| Receive runtime events from a service | module event                          |
1709	| Add an Android permission             | plugin                                |
1710	| Add an Info.plist value               | plugin                                |
1711	| Add a native build dependency         | module package metadata and/or plugin |
1712	
1713	One package may contain both a module and a plugin when it needs runtime code
1714	and project configuration.
1715	
1716	## Discovery and linking
1717	
1718	Module crates opt in with `[package.metadata.whisker]`. CNG walks the
1719	application's Cargo dependency graph during generation and records the native
1720	packages that the generated Host target must link. Android's Gradle plugin and
1721	iOS Swift Package Manager then use their native dependency systems during a
1722	normal Gradle/Xcode build. Web and desktop Host crates are ordinary optional
1723	Cargo dependencies selected for those targets.
1724	
1725	See [Authoring a Module](/docs/authoring-a-module.md) and
1726	[Authoring a Plugin](/docs/authoring-a-plugin.md) for implementation details.
1727	
1728	# How It Works
1729	
1730	A Whisker app is one native process. Your compiled Rust application is loaded as
1731	a library inside the platform application; Whisker does not start a separate
1732	Rust process or keep an independent game loop running.
1733	
1734	The Host creates a runtime instance and drives it in short transactions from its
1735	own event loop. Rust owns UI state and semantics; the Host owns platform
1736	integration and the final pixels.
1737	
1738	## From `render!` to a frame
1739	
1740	`render!` is authoring syntax over public builders. A declaration such as
1741	`View(style: …) { Text(value: …) }` creates a tree of small `Element` handles.
1742	Reactive properties install effects that update the retained scene when their
1743	signals change.
1744	
1745	The frame path is:
1746	
1747	```text
1748	component builders
1749	      ↓
1750	retained element scene
1751	      ↓
1752	typed style resolution + Taffy layout
1753	      ↓  Host measurement when intrinsic size is needed
1754	semantic FramePacket
1755	      ↓
1756	platform Host projection and paint
1757	```
1758	
1759	Rust is authoritative for the element hierarchy, computed style, layout, input
1760	routing, and frame revisions. A `FramePacket` contains semantic operations and
1761	resolved geometry rather than CSS text or platform object pointers. Hosts apply
1762	the packet transactionally:
1763	
1764	- iOS maps elements to UIKit views and platform paint;
1765	- Android maps elements to Android views and platform paint;
1766	- Web maps elements to explicitly positioned DOM nodes;
1767	- Desktop shares a winit/wgpu renderer across macOS, Windows, and Linux code.
1768	
1769	Text and custom Host elements may need an intrinsic size before Taffy can finish
1770	layout. Rust batches measurement requests, the Host returns logical sizes, and
1771	the same surface completes layout before producing the final frame.
1772	
1773	## Event and idle model
1774	
1775	The Host calls the runtime for startup, viewport changes, pointer/touch events,
1776	module events, and animation frames. Event dispatch and signal writes can make
1777	the scene dirty. When Rust-side async completion or reactive work arrives first,
1778	the runtime uses the wake callback supplied at initialization to ask the Host to
1779	schedule another drive.
1780	
1781	When nothing is dirty, no animation is active, and no task is ready, the runtime
1782	does not spin. It remains an in-memory object and waits for the next Host call.
1783	Heavy synchronous Rust work therefore blocks the Host UI thread; use
1784	`run_blocking` for blocking work and return the result through the runtime
1785	dispatcher.
1786	
1787	## One boundary, two bindings
1788	
1789	The core is platform-independent. The boundary branches only at composition:
1790	
1791	- **Android and iOS** cross a narrow C-compatible Driver ABI because Kotlin and
1792	  Swift cannot call Rust traits directly. The Host owns callbacks for frame
1793	  presentation, measurement, wake requests, resources, and modules.
1794	- **Web and Desktop** are Rust Hosts. They instantiate `RuntimeInstance` and
1795	  implement the same measurement and frame-sink concepts with ordinary Rust
1796	  calls, avoiding an unnecessary serialization or FFI layer.
1797	
1798	`WhiskerValue` is the common recursive value type for module arguments, returns,
1799	properties, and event payloads. Built-in `View` and `Text` use the same element
1800	registration and Host-module model as third-party native elements.
1801	
1802	## Build and generated Hosts
1803	
1804	`whisker.rs` is the declarative application configuration. Continuous Native
1805	Generation (CNG) turns it and the Cargo dependency graph into `gen/<platform>/`:
1806	
1807	```text
1808	whisker.rs + Cargo metadata
1809	           ↓
1810	       whisker-cng
1811	           ↓
1812	gen/android  gen/ios  gen/macos  gen/web
1813	```
1814	
1815	The generated tree is a build artifact shared by `whisker run` and `whisker
1816	build`. It contains only the application composition shell; the reusable Host
1817	implementation lives in the platform SDK/library. Android Studio and Xcode can
1818	build their generated projects directly because Gradle/Xcode invoke Whisker's
1819	Rust build adapter as part of the native build graph.
1820	
1821	## Development loop
1822	
1823	`whisker run <platform>` synchronizes CNG output, performs the initial build,
1824	launches the Host, and watches Rust sources. Function-body changes normally
1825	become subsecond patches applied to the loaded Rust library while component
1826	state remains alive. Dependency, signature, or native-project changes require a
1827	full rebuild and relaunch.
1828	
1829	The supported run targets are `android`, `ios`, `web`, and `desktop`. See
1830	[Hot Reload](/docs/hot-reload.md) for patch rules and the
1831	[CLI Reference](/docs/cli-reference.md) for exact commands and flags.
1832	
1833	## Crates application authors see
1834	
1835	Most applications depend only on `whisker` and import
1836	`whisker::prelude::*`. Separate `whisker-*` crates provide routing and native
1837	capabilities. Framework internals are split so that:
1838	
1839	- `whisker-runtime` owns reactivity, element handles, runtime instances, tasks,
1840	  events, and module dispatch;
1841	- `whisker-style`, `whisker-layout`, and `whisker-engine` own structured style,
1842	  Taffy layout, retained scenes, measurement, and frame production;
1843	- `whisker-driver` is only the safe mobile FFI adapter;
1844	- platform libraries own Host projection, measurement, input conversion, and
1845	  paint.
1846	
1847	That split is why a new Host can be implemented without changing application
1848	components: it supplies the boundary callbacks or Rust traits and consumes the
1849	same protocol.
1850	
1851	# Routing
1852	
1853	This guide walks through adding screen-to-screen navigation to a
1854	Whisker app with the `whisker-router` crate. We'll build a small
1855	two-screen flow — a list that pushes a detail screen with a native
1856	slide transition and a working back gesture — then layer on tabs.
1857	
1858	For the complete API surface (every container, transition, and hook),
1859	see the [Routing reference](/docs/routing-api.md). This page is the
1860	fast path to a working router.
1861	
1862	## 1. Add the dependency
1863	
1864	`whisker-router` is a companion crate. Add it to your app's
1865	`Cargo.toml` alongside `whisker`:
1866	
1867	```toml
1868	[dependencies]
1869	whisker = { workspace = true }
1870	whisker-router = "0.12"
1871	```
1872	
1873	Import what you need directly — the crate has no `prelude`:
1874	
1875	```rust
1876	use whisker::prelude::*;
1877	use whisker_router::{
1878	    routes, Router, Outlet,

content.text: Reading Whisker's docs (routing, elements, modules, builds) before scaffolding the app.

content.content:
1878	    routes, Router, Outlet,
1879	    use_navigator, use_param,
1880	};
1881	```
1882	
1883	## 2. Declare the route tree
1884	
1885	Routes are declared with the `routes!` macro. The macro takes a nested
1886	block of **containers** (`Stack`, `Switch`) and **routes** (`Route`)
1887	and produces a `RouteSet` — the compiled tree + component registry the
1888	router needs.
1889	
1890	```rust
1891	routes! {
1892	    Stack {
1893	        Route(path: "", component: Home)
1894	        Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
1895	    }
1896	}
1897	```
1898	
1899	- `Stack` — an ordered container with push/pop history.
1900	- `Route(path:, component:)` — a screen with a URL segment and
1901	  a component.
1902	- `:id` in a path is a dynamic parameter. Read it at render time
1903	  with `use_param("id")`.
1904	
1905	The full grammar is in the
1906	[Routing reference](/docs/routing-api.md#the-routes-macro).
1907	
1908	## 3. Mount the Router
1909	
1910	`Router` takes the route tree, publishes the handle into context, creates a
1911	positioned root container, and installs the current Host's navigation driver.
1912	Inside it, mount an `Outlet` to render the active route:
1913	
1914	```rust
1915	#[whisker::main]
1916	fn app() -> Element {
1917	    render! {
1918	        View(style: css!(
1919	            flex_grow: 1.0,
1920	            width: vw(100),
1921	            height: vh(100),
1922	            display: Display::Flex,
1923	            flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column,
1924	        )) {
1925	            Router(routes: routes! {
1926	                Stack {
1927	                    Route(path: "", component: Home)
1928	                    Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
1929	                }
1930	            }) {
1931	                Outlet {}
1932	            }
1933	        }
1934	    }
1935	}
1936	```
1937	
1938	`Outlet` renders whichever screen the current state points to. Native
1939	navigation input is automatic: Android system/predictive back, iOS edge swipe,
1940	and Web browser history are connected for the lifetime of the `Router`.
1941	
1942	### Advanced: explicit handle
1943	
1944	`Router` builds the `RouterHandle` for you from `routes`. If you need
1945	the handle _before_ the Router mounts — for example, to build a
1946	navigation facade that a feature crate can call into — create it
1947	manually with `RouterHandle::new(...)` and publish it with
1948	`provide_router(handle)`:
1949	
1950	```rust
1951	let handle = RouterHandle::new(routes! { /* ... */ });
1952	// use handle for pre-mount logic...
1953	provide_router(handle);
1954	```
1955	
1956	## 4. Navigate
1957	
1958	From any component inside the `Router`, call `use_navigator()` to get
1959	the handle and navigate by URL:
1960	
1961	```rust
1962	#[component]
1963	fn home() -> Element {
1964	    let nav = use_navigator();
1965	    render! {
1966	        View(style: css!(
1967	            flex_grow: 1.0,
1968	            display: Display::Flex,
1969	            flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column,
1970	            justify_content: JustifyContent::Center,
1971	            align_items: AlignItems::Center,
1972	        )) {
1973	            Text(value: "Items")
1974	            View(on_tap: move |_| {
1975	                let _ = nav.navigate("/detail/1");
1976	            }) {
1977	                Text(value: "Open item 1")
1978	            }
1979	            View(on_tap: move |_| {
1980	                let _ = nav.navigate("/detail/2");
1981	            }) {
1982	                Text(value: "Open item 2")
1983	            }
1984	        }
1985	    }
1986	}
1987	```
1988	
1989	The six navigation operations:
1990	
1991	| Call                         | Effect                                                              |
1992	| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
1993	| `nav.navigate("/detail/42")` | Push a new screen onto the active Stack                             |
1994	| `nav.back()`                 | Pop the top of the deepest active Stack                             |
1995	| `nav.select("/(home)")`      | Switch a tab (change Switch branch)                                 |
1996	| `nav.replace("/other")`      | Swap the top entry (same Stack only)                                |
1997	| `nav.pop_to("/")`            | Pop until the target is on top (same Stack only)                    |
1998	| `nav.reset("/")`             | **Global** — clear _every_ back stack and go to the target (logout) |
1999	
2000	All targets are plain URL strings. Dynamic `:param` segments are
2001	extracted automatically by matching against the route tree.
2002	
2003	`reset` is the odd one out: `replace` and `pop_to` only touch the current
2004	Stack, but `reset` rebuilds the whole navigation state onto a single clean
2005	path to the target — switching tabs toward it and clearing the back stack of
2006	_every_ Stack. A URL resolves to a **leaf screen**, and `/` is the home index
2007	screen (reachable from any tab); group segments like `(home)` are optional.
2008	
2009	## 5. Read route params
2010	
2011	A component mounted under a `Route(path: "detail/:id", ...)` reads its
2012	`:id` with `use_param`:
2013	
2014	```rust
2015	#[component]
2016	fn detail() -> Element {
2017	    let nav = use_navigator();
2018	    let id = use_param("id");
2019	
2020	    render! {
2021	        View(style: css!(
2022	            flex_grow: 1.0,
2023	            display: Display::Flex,
2024	            flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column,
2025	            justify_content: JustifyContent::Center,
2026	            align_items: AlignItems::Center,
2027	        )) {
2028	            Text(value: format!("Detail #{}", id.get().unwrap_or_default()))
2029	            View(on_tap: move |_| { let _ = nav.back(); }) {
2030	                Text(value: "Back")
2031	            }
2032	        }
2033	    }
2034	}
2035	```
2036	
2037	`use_param` returns a `ReadSignal<Option<String>>` that updates when
2038	the route's params change.
2039	
2040	## 6. Add tabs
2041	
2042	Tabs use two additional concepts: **Switch** (a parallel container that
2043	keeps all branches alive) and **layout routes** (a `Route` with both a
2044	component and children).
2045	
2046	```text
2047	Route(component: TabsLayout)            ← layout: tab bar chrome + Outlet
2048	  └─ Switch
2049	       ├─ Route(path: "(home)")         ← group: no URL segment
2050	       │    └─ Stack
2051	       │         ├─ Route("", Home)
2052	       │         └─ Route("detail/:id", Detail)
2053	       └─ Route(path: "(search)")
2054	            └─ Stack
2055	                 ├─ Route("list", ListScreen)
2056	                 └─ Route("detail/:id", Detail)
2057	```
2058	
2059	The tree declares a `Switch` inside a layout route. Each tab branch
2060	has its own `Stack`, so each tab has independent push/pop history.
2061	
2062	```rust
2063	Router(routes: routes! {
2064	    Route(component: TabsLayout) {
2065	        Switch {
2066	            Route(path: "(home)") {
2067	                Stack {
2068	                    Route(path: "", component: Home)
2069	                    Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
2070	                }
2071	            }
2072	            Route(path: "(search)") {
2073	                Stack {
2074	                    Route(path: "list", component: ListScreen)
2075	                    Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
2076	                }
2077	            }
2078	        }
2079	    }
2080	}) {
2081	    Outlet {}
2082	}
2083	```
2084	
2085	### Layout routes
2086	
2087	`Route(component: TabsLayout)` is a **layout route**: it has a
2088	component _and_ children. The component renders shared chrome (a tab
2089	bar) with an `Outlet` for the active child. This is the same concept
2090	as Expo Router's `_layout.tsx`.
2091	
2092	```rust
2093	#[component]
2094	fn tabs_layout() -> Element {
2095	    let nav = use_navigator();
2096	    render! {
2097	        View(style: css!(
2098	            flex_grow: 1.0,
2099	            display: Display::Flex,
2100	            flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column,
2101	        )) {
2102	            // Content area
2103	            View(style: css!(flex_grow: 1.0)) {
2104	                Outlet {}
2105	            }
2106	            // Tab bar
2107	            View(style: css!(
2108	                display: Display::Flex,
2109	                flex_direction: FlexDirection::Row,
2110	                justify_content: JustifyContent::SpaceAround,
2111	                height: px(56),
2112	            )) {
2113	                View(on_tap: move |_| { let _ = nav.select("/(home)"); }) {
2114	                    Text(value: "Home")
2115	                }
2116	                View(on_tap: {
2117	                    let nav = nav.clone();
2118	                    move |_| { let _ = nav.select("/(search)"); }
2119	                }) {
2120	                    Text(value: "Search")
2121	                }
2122	            }
2123	        }
2124	    }
2125	}
2126	```
2127	
2128	### Group routes
2129	
2130	`Route(path: "(home)")` is a **group route** — the parenthesised path
2131	appears in the canonical URL (`/(home)/detail/1`) but is **optional
2132	during matching**. `navigate("/detail/1")` still matches because
2133	`(home)` is skipped when absent from the input.
2134	
2135	Group routes organize the tree (each is a Switch branch) without
2136	forcing every URL to spell them out. Use `select("/(home)")` to
2137	explicitly switch to a tab.
2138	
2139	## Route nesting ≠ URL nesting
2140	
2141	This is the most important concept to understand about the route tree.
2142	Nesting a `Route` inside another `Route` creates a **layout
2143	relationship**, not a pushable screen. The parent must render an
2144	`Outlet` for the child to appear, and `back()` does not pop the child.
2145	
2146	```rust
2147	// WRONG — Detail is a child of Home (layout relationship).
2148	// navigate() modifies the child state in-place; back() does not pop.
2149	Stack {
2150	    Route(path: "", component: Home) {
2151	        Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
2152	    }
2153	}
2154	
2155	// CORRECT — Home and Detail are siblings in the Stack.
2156	// navigate() pushes Detail; back() pops to Home.
2157	Stack {
2158	    Route(path: "", component: Home)
2159	    Route(path: "detail/:id", component: Detail)
2160	}
2161	```
2162	
2163	To share a URL prefix among pushable screens, spell the full path on
2164	each sibling:
2165	
2166	```rust
2167	Stack {
2168	    Route(path: "settings", component: Settings)
2169	    Route(path: "settings/account", component: Account)
2170	    Route(path: "settings/privacy", component: Privacy)
2171	}
2172	```
2173	
2174	Reserve `Route` nesting for layout routes (tab bars, headers, drawers)
2175	where the parent renders shared UI around an `Outlet`.
2176	
2177	## Run it
2178	
2179	```bash
2180	whisker run ios
2181	```
2182	
2183	Tap a row to push the detail screen with a native slide animation;
2184	swipe from the left edge (or tap Back) to pop it. Push/pop history is
2185	preserved per-tab.
