2196	# Using First-party Modules
2197	
2198	Whisker keeps the core small. Native widgets and platform services ship
2199	as separate crates you add to `Cargo.toml` on demand — each a thin,
2200	typed Rust wrapper over a Host module that you consume the same way from app
2201	code. Check the module's Rustdoc for its current platform coverage; not every
2202	device API has a meaningful implementation on every Host.
2203	
2204	This guide is a set of short recipes: for each crate, what to add to
2205	`Cargo.toml` and a minimal example. For the full prop and method
2206	surface of every module, see the
2207	[First-party Modules reference](/docs/modules-api.md).
2208	
2209	All examples assume the prelude is in scope:
2210	
2211	```rust
2212	use whisker::prelude::*;
2213	```
2214	
2215	These crates live in the Whisker workspace, so a path dependency is the
2216	usual way to depend on them:
2217	
2218	```toml
2219	[dependencies]
2220	whisker-image = "0.12"
2221	```
2222	
2223	## Images — `whisker-image`
2224	
2225	`Image` loads and caches a remote bitmap from the native module
2226	(Kingfisher on iOS, Coil on Android). Set the `mode` prop to control
2227	how the image fits its box.
2228	
2229	```toml
2230	[dependencies]
2231	whisker-image = "0.12"
2232	```
2233	
2234	```rust
2235	use whisker_image::{Image, ImageMode};
2236	
2237	render! {
2238	    Image(
2239	        src: "https://example.com/cover.jpg",
2240	        mode: ImageMode::AspectFill,
2241	        style: css!(width: px(240), height: px(240), border_radius: px(8)),
2242	    )
2243	}
2244	```
2245	
2246	`mode` defaults to `ImageMode::AspectFill`. The other variants are
2247	`AspectFit`, `ScaleToFill`, and `Center`. All props are reactive —
2248	swap `src` to re-fetch, swap `mode` to re-lay-out without a remount.
2249	Width and height must be set (here via `style`, or let flex size it).
2250	
2251	## Icons — `whisker-icons`
2252	
2253	`Icon` renders a Lucide icon. Each icon is its own `pub const &str`
2254	holding the full SVG markup, under the `lucide` module — so unused
2255	icons are stripped from your binary by the linker.
2256	
2257	```toml
2258	[dependencies]
2259	whisker-icons = "0.12"
2260	```
2261	
2262	```rust
2263	use whisker_icons::{Icon, lucide};
2264	
2265	render! {
2266	    Icon(svg: lucide::Heart, color: "#ff5577", size: "24")
2267	}
2268	```
2269	
2270	Reference any of the ~1700 PascalCase constants by name
2271	(`lucide::ChevronRight`, `lucide::Search`, `lucide::X`, …). `color` is
2272	substituted for `currentColor` (Lucide draws with
2273	`stroke="currentColor"`). `size` is the square edge length — a bare
2274	number like `"24"` is treated as `px`; a value with a unit (`"1.5em"`,
2275	`"100%"`) passes through.
2276	
2277	## Inline SVG — `whisker-svg`
2278	
2279	`Svg` renders arbitrary SVG XML. It compiles the markup to a
2280	display-list byte stream in Rust and streams it to a native replayer.
2281	
2282	```toml
2283	[dependencies]
2284	whisker-svg = "0.12"
2285	```
2286	
2287	```rust
2288	use whisker_svg::Svg;
2289	
2290	render! {
2291	    Svg(
2292	        content: r#"<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24">
2293	            <path d="M 5 12 L 10 17 L 19 7"
2294	                  stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/>
2295	        </svg>"#,
2296	        color: "#1d9bf0",
2297	        style: css!(width: px(24), height: px(24)),
2298	    )
2299	}
2300	```
2301	
2302	The `content` must contain a top-level `<svg>` with a `viewBox`; an
2303	empty string renders nothing. `color` replaces any
2304	`fill="currentColor"` / `stroke="currentColor"` paint. As with `Image`,
2305	width and height must be set via `style` (or flex).
2306	
2307	## Video — `whisker-video`
2308	
2309	`Video` is a native playback element (AVPlayer / Media3 ExoPlayer)
2310	with imperative controls. You drive play/pause/seek through a
2311	`VideoHandle`, bound to the element on mount via the
2312	[`element_ref:`](/docs/refs.md) pattern.
2313	
2314	```toml
2315	[dependencies]
2316	whisker-video = "0.12"
2317	```
2318	
2319	```rust
2320	use whisker_video::{Video, VideoHandle};
2321	
2322	let video = VideoHandle::new();
2323	
2324	render! {
2325	    View(style: css!(flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column)) {
2326	        Video(
2327	            element_ref: video.r(),
2328	            src: "https://example.com/clip.mp4",
2329	            style: css!(width: percent(100), height: px(240)),
2330	        )
2331	        View(style: css!(flex_direction: FlexDirection::Row)) {
2332	            Text(value: "play",  on_tap: move |_| video.play())
2333	            Text(value: "pause", on_tap: move |_| video.pause())
2334	            Text(value: "+10s",  on_tap: move |_| video.seek(10.0))
2335	        }
2336	    }
2337	}
2338	```
2339	
2340	Create the handle with `VideoHandle::new()`, pass `video.r()` to the
2341	element's `element_ref:` prop, then call `play()`, `pause()`, or
2342	`seek(seconds)` from any handler. `VideoHandle` is `Copy`, so each
2343	`move ||` closure captures its own copy — no `clone()` needed.
2344	
2345	## Audio — `whisker-audio`
2346	
2347	`Player` is a view-less audio engine (AVPlayer / Media3 ExoPlayer). It
2348	drives playback and exposes a reactive `PlaybackStatus` signal — there
2349	is no element to mount.
2350	
2351	```toml
2352	[dependencies]
2353	whisker-audio = "0.12"
2354	```
2355	
2356	```rust
2357	use whisker_audio::Player;
2358	
2359	let player = Player::new("https://example.com/clip.mp3");
2360	let status = player.status();
2361	
2362	render! {
2363	    View(style: css!(flex_direction: FlexDirection::Column, padding: px(16))) {
2364	        Text(value: computed(move || format!(
2365	            "{:.1}s / {:.1}s",
2366	            status.get().position,
2367	            status.get().duration,
2368	        )))
2369	        View(on_tap: {
2370	            let p = player.clone();
2371	            move |_| p.play()
2372	        }) {
2373	            Text(value: "play")
2374	        }
2375	    }
2376	}
2377	```
2378	
2379	Construct with `Player::new(source)` (HTTP/HTTPS or `file://`). The
2380	methods (`play`, `pause`, `stop`, `seek_to`, `set_source`,
2381	`set_volume`, `set_loop`) are fire-and-forget — state surfaces through
2382	the `status()` signal, not return values. `Player` is `Clone`
2383	(`Rc`-backed); every clone shares the same native player and the same
2384	status signal, so the example clones the handle into the tap closure.
2385	
2386	### Permissions and background mode
2387	
2388	To record audio or keep playback alive in the background, register the
2389	crate's `WhiskerAudio` plugin in your `whisker.rs`. The plugin
2390	contributes the matching `Info.plist` / `AndroidManifest.xml` entries:
2391	
2392	```rust
2393	// whisker.rs
2394	fn main() {
2395	    whisker_cng::run(|app| {
2396	        app.name("Podcast")
2397	            .bundle_id("rs.whisker.podcast");
2398	
2399	        app.plugin::<whisker_audio::WhiskerAudio>(|c| {
2400	            c.microphone_permission("Record clips for podcast episodes.")
2401	                .record_audio_android(true)
2402	                .enable_background_playback(true);
2403	        });
2404	    });
2405	}
2406	```
2407	
2408	| Setter                              | Effect                                       |
2409	| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
2410	| `microphone_permission(text)`       | Sets `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` (iOS)    |
2411	| `record_audio_android(true)`        | Adds `android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO`       |
2412	| `enable_background_recording(true)` | Adds `"audio"` to iOS `UIBackgroundModes`    |
2413	| `enable_background_playback(true)`  | Same `UIBackgroundModes` entry, for playback |
2414	
2415	See [Configuration](/docs/configuration-api.md) for the `whisker.rs`
2416	file and how plugins are registered.
2417	
2418	## Safe-area insets — `whisker-safe-area`
2419	
2420	`safe_area_insets()` returns a reactive `ReadSignal<SafeAreaInsets>`
2421	for the host view's insets (notch, Dynamic Island, status bar, home
2422	indicator, navigation bar). Read it inside a reactive style to pad your
2423	layout around the unsafe edges.
2424	
2425	```toml
2426	[dependencies]
2427	whisker-safe-area = "0.12"
2428	```
2429	
2430	```rust
2431	use whisker_safe_area::safe_area_insets;
2432	
2433	let insets = safe_area_insets();
2434	let outer_style = move || {
2435	    let i = insets.get();
2436	    format!(
2437	        "padding-top: {}px; padding-bottom: {}px; \
2438	         padding-left: {}px; padding-right: {}px;",
2439	        i.top, i.bottom, i.leading, i.trailing,
2440	    )
2441	};
2442	
2443	render! {
2444	    View(style: outer_style()) {
2445	        // your content
2446	    }
2447	}
2448	```
2449	
2450	The struct fields are `top`, `bottom`, `leading`, and `trailing`
2451	(`leading == left`, `trailing == right` for LTR), in points (iOS) / dp
2452	(Android) — the same units as Whisker's CSS `px` literals. Every call
2453	hands back the same process-global signal, so reading it from many
2454	components is cheap. **Call it from the main thread.**
2455	
2456	## Local storage — `whisker-local-store`
2457	
2458	`WhiskerLocalStore` is a persistent, string-keyed key-value store
2459	(`UserDefaults` on iOS, `SharedPreferences` on Android). It's for small
2460	state — not large blobs — and persists across launches but doesn't sync
2461	across devices.
2462	
2463	```toml
2464	[dependencies]
2465	whisker-local-store = "0.12"
2466	```
2467	
2468	```rust
2469	use whisker_local_store::WhiskerLocalStore;
2470	
2471	// save / load / remove are associated functions — no instance to build.
2472	let _ = WhiskerLocalStore::save("user_id".into(), "abc".into())?;
2473	
2474	let loaded = WhiskerLocalStore::load("user_id".into())?;
2475	// -> Some("abc".to_string())
2476	
2477	let _ = WhiskerLocalStore::remove("user_id".into())?;
2478	```
2479	
2480	Each call returns a `Result` (`save` yields `bool`, `load` yields
2481	`Option<String>`, `remove` yields `()`). Call from anywhere the
2482	reactive runtime runs — component bodies, event handlers, or effects.

2493	# Authoring a Module
2494	
2495	A module package keeps its shared Rust API at the root and places each Host
2496	implementation beside it:
2497

3064 # App Configuration 3065 3066 Every Whisker app carries a `whisker.rs` file next to its `Cargo.toml`. 3067 Its `main` function calls `whisker_cng::run` to configure the app and generate 3068 platform projects. CNG discovers modules, builds and applies native generation 3069 plugins, and writes the Host projects under `gen/`. Every execution performs 3070 generation; unchanged projects reuse their fingerprints. 3071 3072 This page is the practical how-to. The exhaustive field-by-field 3073 reference is in [Configuration](/docs/configuration-api.md). 3074 3075 ## The configuration entry point 3076 3077 Configure the app inside the closure passed to `whisker_cng::run`. Every 3078 builder method returns `&mut Self`, so calls chain, and the `ios`, `android`, and `plugin` 3079 methods each take a closure receiving a mutable reference to the nested 3080 config: 3081 3082 ```rust 3083 fn main() { 3084 whisker_cng::run(|app| { 3085 app.name("MyApp") 3086 .bundle_id("dev.example.myapp") 3087 .version("1.0.0") 3088 .build_number(1); 3089 }); 3090 } 3091 ``` 3092 3093 ## Cargo registration and editor support 3094 3095 `whisker new` registers `whisker.rs` as a binary in your application's 3096 `Cargo.toml`: 3097 3098 ```toml 3099 [[bin]] 3100 name = "whisker-config" 3101 path = "whisker.rs" 3102 required-features = ["whisker-config"] 3103 test = false 3104 bench = false 3105 3106 [features] 3107 whisker-config = ["whisker-cng/generate"] 3108 ``` 3109 3110 The application also depends on `whisker-cng` with `default-features = false`, 3111 using the version provided by the CLI template. The `whisker-config` feature 3112 enables its generation engine. Normal application builds omit that engine, 3113 including Cargo dependency discovery and image processing. 3114 3115 Rust-analyzer discovers the file through Cargo, so completion and navigation 3116 work without `linkedProjects` or a separate configuration package. Configuration 3117 types and the `run` interface remain available with the feature disabled. 3118 Add plugin crates with `cargo add`, then use their configuration APIs in 3119 `whisker.rs`. No second dependency list needs to be maintained. 3120 3121 To generate an Xcode project from the application directory: 3122 3123 ```sh 3124 cargo run --bin whisker-config --features whisker-config -- ios 3125 ``` 3126 3127 Pass `android`, `desktop`, or `web` for another platform. Omit the platform to 3128 generate all four projects, or pass multiple names to generate a subset. 3129 `--manifest-path ` after Cargo's `--` selects an 3130 application explicitly. These directories are CNG output shared by `run` and `build`. Do not hand-edit them; express persistent configuration in `whisker.rs`, module metadata, or a plugin. ## Android release The Android host project is a plain Gradle app. Build a release APK straight from `gen/android/`: ```sh ( cd gen/android && ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease ) ``` The APK lands at: ``` gen/android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk ``` For Play Store upload you usually want an Android App Bundle instead: ```sh ( cd gen/android && ./gradlew :app:bundleRelease ) # → gen/android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab ``` ### Signing An unsigned release build is not installable. Wire up a Gradle `signingConfig` the standard Android way, in `gen/android/app/build.gradle.kts`: ```kotlin android { signingConfigs { create("release") { storeFile = file(System.getenv("WHISKER_KEYSTORE") ?: "release.keystore") storePassword = System.getenv("WHISKER_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD") keyAlias = System.getenv("WHISKER_KEY_ALIAS") keyPassword = System.getenv("WHISKER_KEY_PASSWORD") } } buildTypes { getByName("release") { signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release") } } } ``` Because `gen/android/` is generated output, treat its `build.gradle.kts` as disposable. Persistent signing customization belongs in the credential flow or a plugin: - Inject signing from a [plugin](/docs/plugin-api.md) so it's reapplied every time the project is generated. For the supported credential workflow, run `whisker build appbundle --help` or `whisker credential --help`. ## iOS release The iOS host is a normal Xcode project, so you build it with `xcodebuild`. The key distinction is **Simulator vs device**: a release you can submit must be a device (arm64) build, not a Simulator build. Build a Release configuration for a connected device: ```sh ( cd gen/ios && xcodebuild \ -project MyApp.xcodeproj \ -scheme MyApp \ -configuration Release \ -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \ build ) ``` For App Store submission, archive instead of plain `build`: ```sh ( cd gen/ios && xcodebuild \ -project MyApp.xcodeproj \ -scheme MyApp \ -configuration Release \ -destination 'generic/platform=iOS' \ -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive \ archive ) ``` Then export an `.ipa` from the archive with `xcodebuild -exportArchive` and your `ExportOptions.plist`, the standard Apple flow. ### Code signing Device builds require a signing identity and a provisioning profile. Provide them to `xcodebuild` the usual way: ```sh xcodebuild ... \ DEVELOPMENT_TEAM=ABCDE12345 \ CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Automatic ``` > **Important caveat.** `gen/ios/` is regenerated on every > `whisker run`. Any signing configuration baked into the generated > Xcode project — team IDs, provisioning specifiers, entitlements — is > lost on the next regeneration. Don't hand-edit the generated > `.xcodeproj` and expect it to stick. Manage signing one of these ways instead: - Pass `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` / `CODE_SIGN_STYLE` on the `xcodebuild` command line (as above), so nothing needs to persist in the project. - Apply signing from a [plugin](/docs/plugin-api.md) that re-runs on every generation. `whisker build ipa --help` documents the supported export and credential options; Xcode remains available for custom archive workflows. ## The iOS SwiftPM runtime dependency You rarely need to touch this — it matters only when bumping Whisker — but it's worth understanding what your iOS app actually depends on. The generated iOS project doesn't vendor Whisker's Swift runtime. It resolves `WhiskerRuntime` (and the companion Swift targets) from the remote **`whisker` SwiftPM package**, pinned to a git tag. The version is defined once in the CNG implementation: ```rust // crates/whisker-cng/src/ios_modules.rs pub const WHISKER_IOS_SPM_URL: &str = "https://github.com/whiskerrs/whisker.git"; pub const WHISKER_IOS_SPM_VERSION: &str = "..."; ``` That constant drives the `XCRemoteSwiftPackageReference` the generator writes into your project. It must stay compatible with the published Swift package tag and with module `Package.swift` pins. The release process also keeps the Rust crates, Android SDK, and Gradle plugin compatible. Consult the release notes for exact versions instead of copying a static matrix from this guide. For most app authors this is invisible: you install a `whisker-cli` version, and the iOS package version it pins comes along for the ride. You only deal with those pins when you're the one releasing Whisker. ## App Store / Play submission `whisker` produces a **normal native app** — a signed AAB and a signed `.ipa` — and can upload it for you: ```sh whisker submit ios whisker submit android ``` [Store Submission](/docs/store-submission.md) covers uploading builds, the credentials each store needs, and managing your store listing — descriptions, screenshots, release notes — from a `store.rs` file. The artifacts are also ordinary store uploads, so Xcode Organizer, Transporter, or the Play Console work too. Both stores require an app icon. Set one with the built-in `AppIcon` plugin — see [App Configuration](/docs/app-configuration.md#step-5-app-icon). Without it, submission fails validation (iOS rejects the missing icon; Play requires a launcher icon). See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference.md) for the development commands that produce the `gen/` projects these builds run against.

4139	`eprintln!`, and the `log` crate — appears right there:
4140	
4141	```rust

4143	
4144	fn on_tap() {
4145	    println!("tapped at {:?}", std::time::Instant::now());
4146	}
4147	```
4148	
4149	You do **not** need a separate `logcat` window (Android) or Console
4150	session (iOS) just to read your own prints — the run loop already pulls
4151	them in. The native-side firehose is suppressed by default so your logs
4152	aren't buried; see [native logs](#native-side-logs) below to opt back
4153	in.
4154	
4155	## How panics behave
4156	
4157	Whisker contains panics at the FFI boundary so a single bad `unwrap()`
4158	doesn't take the whole app down. The runtime wraps the two places user
4159	code crosses the C ABI in `catch_unwind`:
4160	
4161	- **Frame ticks.** The per-frame reactive flush runs under
4162	  `catch_unwind`. A panic there drops that frame — the app keeps
4163	  running, and the runtime's internal guards keep reactive state
4164	  consistent so the next tick proceeds cleanly.
4165	- **Event handlers.** A panic in an `on_tap` / `on_<event>` handler is
4166	  caught, the event is dropped (reported as "not consumed" so the
4167	  native chain can fall back), and the app continues.
4168	
4169	Either way the panic is **logged** — the message reaches stderr via the
4170	default panic hook and is forwarded to your `whisker run` terminal. So a

4208	run the doctor:
4209	
4210	```sh

4212	```
4213	
4214	It inspects your local setup and reports what's missing or

# Debugging & Logging

Most of what you need while building a Whisker app shows up in the
terminal you ran `whisker run` from. This guide covers where your logs
go, how the runtime behaves when something panics, and which native
tools to reach for when the problem is below the Rust layer.

## App logs in the run terminal

`whisker run` captures the device's stdout/stderr and forwards it to the
terminal it's running in. That means your app's own output — `println!`,
`eprintln!`, and the `log` crate — appears right there:

```rust
use whisker::prelude::*;

fn on_tap() {
    println!("tapped at {:?}", std::time::Instant::now());
}
```

You do **not** need a separate `logcat` window (Android) or Console
session (iOS) just to read your own prints — the run loop already pulls
them in. The native-side firehose is suppressed by default so your logs
aren't buried; see [native logs](#native-side-logs) below to opt back
in.

## How panics behave

Whisker contains panics at the FFI boundary so a single bad `unwrap()`
doesn't take the whole app down. The runtime wraps the two places user
code crosses the C ABI in `catch_unwind`:

- **Frame ticks.** The per-frame reactive flush runs under
  `catch_unwind`. A panic there drops that frame — the app keeps
  running, and the runtime's internal guards keep reactive state
  consistent so the next tick proceeds cleanly.
- **Event handlers.** A panic in an `on_tap` / `on_<event>` handler is
  caught, the event is dropped (reported as "not consumed" so the
  native chain can fall back), and the app continues.

Either way the panic is **logged** — the message reaches stderr via the
default panic hook and is forwarded to your `whisker run` terminal. So a
panic shows up as a logged message and a dropped frame or event, not a
crash.

> This is contain-and-continue, not silently-ignore. If something isn't
> rendering or a tap does nothing, check the run terminal for a panic
> message before assuming a logic bug.

## Native-side logs

When the problem is below your application Rust — Host painting, the
Swift/Kotlin shell, or a native module — enable verbose output or use the
platform log tools.

Show the underlying build and device streams with verbose mode:

```sh
whisker --verbose run ios
WHISKER_VERBOSE=1 whisker run android
```

Or go straight to the platform tools in a separate terminal:

```sh
# Android
adb logcat

# iOS Simulator
xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream
```

These show Host diagnostics, native crashes, and system messages that are too
noisy for the default TUI.

## Environment problems

If the toolchain itself is the problem — a missing Rust target, an
Android NDK/SDK/JDK that isn't where it should be, an Xcode that's off —
run the doctor:

```sh
whisker doctor
```

It inspects your local setup and reports what's missing or
misconfigured. Use `--no-ios` / `--no-android` to skip a platform you
don't care about.

**The UI stops updating after patching in a local Whisker.** When you point
an app at a Whisker checkout with `[patch.crates-io]`, patch every Whisker
crate the app depends on, not only `whisker`. A crate left on crates.io pulls
in its own `whisker-runtime`, and a signal from one copy never notifies a
reader in the other: the screen just doesn't change, and nothing is logged.
`cargo tree --duplicates` lists `whisker-runtime` twice when this happens.

## More output

One global knob turns up the verbosity:

- `--verbose` / `WHISKER_VERBOSE=1` — show every step's full underlying
  output (raw `cargo` / `xcodebuild` / `simctl` streams and internal
  debug logs). It's global, applies to any subcommand, and subprocesses
  inherit the env var.

## Known gap

There is **no on-device red-box error overlay yet**. When something
panics, the signal is in the logs (the run terminal, or the native log
streams above) — not a banner on the screen. Keep the run terminal in
view while iterating.

See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference.md) for every flag mentioned
here.

# Local Modules & Plugins

An app-private module has the same shape as a published module. Put it in the
workspace and add an ordinary path dependency:

```text
my-app/
├── Cargo.toml
├── app/
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src/lib.rs
└── modules/
    └── camera/
        ├── Cargo.toml
        ├── src/lib.rs
        ├── android/
        ├── ios/
        ├── desktop/
        └── web/
```

```toml
[dependencies]
camera = { path = "../modules/camera" }
```

The module manifest still needs the discovery marker:

```toml
[package.metadata.whisker]
```

Regenerate after adding, removing, or moving a module dependency:

```sh
whisker run android
# or explicitly regenerate through the normal build/run workflow
```

CNG owns dependency-graph discovery. A clean checkout therefore needs a
generation step before opening the generated Xcode or Gradle project, just as
it does after changing app configuration. Once generated, Xcode/Gradle perform
the actual native compilation and linking without a surrounding `whisker run`
process.

Use the same `whisker new-module` scaffold and APIs documented in
[Authoring a Module](/docs/authoring-a-module.md). Do not place Host declarations
inside the app's `src/lib.rs`; keeping them in a module crate lets every target
select only its own implementation.

Local plugins likewise use an ordinary path dependency. They mutate CNG's
project IR during generation and must not contain runtime application logic.

# API Reference: Overview & Prelude

4516	# API Reference: Elements
4517	
4518	Elements are retained scene nodes represented in application code by a small,
4519	runtime-local `Element` handle. Built-ins expose PascalCase builders and use the
4520	same common builder contract as Host module elements.
4521	
4522	```rust
4523	render! {
4524	    View(style: css!(padding: px(16))) {
4525	        Text(value: "Hello")
4526	    }
4527	}
4528	```
4529	
4530	This is shorthand for calls ending in `.build()`. Application code normally
4531	imports all built-ins through `whisker::prelude::*`.
4532	
4533	## Built-ins
4534	
4535	### `View`
4536	
4537	The general rectangular container and interaction target. It accepts ordinary
4538	element children and is the default choice for grouping, flex/grid layout,
4539	backgrounds, borders, clipping, and pointer handlers.
4540	
4541	```rust
4542	View::builder()
4543	    .style(css!(padding: px(16)))
4544	    .on_tap(|event| println!("{:?}", event.detail))
4545	    .body(|body| body.push(Text::builder().value("Open").build()))
4546	    .build()
4547	```
4548	
4549	### `Text`
4550	
4551	A measured plain-text leaf. `value` accepts `Into<Signal<String>>`, so a string,
4552	`ReadSignal<String>`, `RwSignal<String>`, or computed signal can drive it.
4553	Typography and color are structured style properties.
4554	
4555	| Method      | Value                  | Notes                        |
4556	| ----------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------- |
4557	| `value`     | `Into<Signal<String>>` | Required text content        |
4558	| `max_lines` | `Into<Signal<u32>>`    | `0` restores unlimited lines |
4559	
4560	Raw text nodes are runtime implementation details and are not public element
4561	tags.
4562	
4563	### `ScrollView`
4564	
4565	A fully mounted scrollable container. Use it for bounded content, carousels, and
4566	pagers; use `List` for large data sets that need Rust-owned virtualization.
4567	
4568	| Method             | Value                      | Notes                                                |
4569	| ------------------ | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
4570	| `axis`             | `ScrollAxis` or signal     | Vertical by default                                  |
4571	| `snap`             | `ScrollSnap` or signal     | Start, center, end, or custom item anchor            |
4572	| `scroll_snap_stop` | `ScrollSnapStop` or signal | `Always` advances at most one snap point per gesture |
4573	| `scroll_enabled`   | `bool` or signal           | Disables user scrolling, not imperative commands     |
4574	| `on_scroll`        | `Fn(ScrollEvent)`          | Current offset, content size, delta, and drag state  |
4575	
4576	```rust
4577	render! {
4578	    ScrollView(
4579	        axis: ScrollAxis::Horizontal,
4580	        snap: ScrollSnap::start(),
4581	        scroll_snap_stop: ScrollSnapStop::Always,
4582	    ) {
4583	        /* pages */
4584	    }
4585	}
4586	```
4587	
4588	### `List`
4589	
4590	A Rust control primitive that virtualizes ordinary element subtrees inside a
4591	standard `ScrollView`. It is not a special Host view and does not accept a body;
4592	`each`, `key`, and `children` are required type-stated render props.
4593	
4594	```rust
4595	render! {
4596	    List(
4597	        style: css!(flex_grow: 1.0),
4598	        content_style: css!(row_gap: px(8)),
4599	        each: move || rows.get(),
4600	        key: |row: &Row| row.id,
4601	        children: |row: ReadSignal<Row>| render! { RowView(row: row) },
4602	    )
4603	}
4604	```
4605	
4606	`style` applies to the scroll viewport; `content_style` applies to the inner
4607	layout track. Additional methods include `axis`, `scroll_enabled`,
4608	`start_reached_threshold`, `end_reached_threshold`, `on_start_reached`,
4609	`on_end_reached`, `header`, `footer`, `empty`, `on_scroll`, `list_ref`, and
4610	`initial_scroll`.
4611	
4612	Items need no estimated or fixed-size API. The virtualizer learns measured
4613	geometry and preserves stable-key state while a key remains mounted. Items that
4614	leave the window dispose their owner; when mounted again they start with fresh
4615	local state. See [Lists & Conditionals](/docs/lists-and-conditionals.md).
4616	
4617	### `Fragment`
4618	
4619	A transparent grouping node. It exists in the Rust mirror but is not forwarded
4620	as a Host view, so it has no style, accessibility, attributes, or event methods.
4621	Its children are hoisted to the nearest real ancestor in source order.
4622	
4623	## Common `ElementBuilder` methods
4624	
4625	`View`, `Text`, `ScrollView`, `List`, and `#[module_element]` builders share the
4626	following surface unless a control primitive intentionally restricts it.
4627	
4628	### Presentation and semantics
4629	
4630	| Method          | Purpose                                                   |
4631	| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
4632	| `style`         | Structured `Css`, `ReadSignal<Css>`, or `RwSignal<Css>`   |
4633	| `id`            | Stable identifier surfaced in event target metadata       |
4634	| `dataset`       | Structured application metadata surfaced on event targets |
4635	| `accessibility` | Role, label/value/hint, state, and related semantics      |
4636	| `element_ref`   | Bind an `ElementRef` for mounted commands                 |
4637	| `child`         | Append one already-built child in direct builder code     |
4638	
4639	`hit_slop`, class names, raw attributes, and raw CSS escape hatches are not part
4640	of the public contract.
4641	
4642	### Pointer and touch events
4643	
4644	Each common event has bubble and capture variants. A `*_catch` listener stops
4645	propagation at that point.
4646	
4647	- `on_tap`, `on_tap_catch`, `on_capture_tap`,
4648	  `on_capture_tap_catch`
4649	- the same four forms for `click`, `touchstart`, `touchmove`, `touchend`, and
4650	  `touchcancel`
4651	
4652	Handlers receive a typed `TouchEvent`. Hit testing and propagation happen in
4653	the retained Rust scene, giving every Host the same phase and stop semantics.
4654	
4655	### Animation lifecycle
4656	
4657	- `on_animationstart`
4658	- `on_animationend`
4659	- `on_animationcancel`
4660	- `on_animationiteration`
4661	- `on_transitionstart`
4662	- `on_transitionend`
4663	- `on_transitioncancel`
4664	
4665	These handlers receive `AnimationEvent`; the timeline and lifecycle generation
4666	are shared Rust behavior rather than Host animation callbacks.
4667	
4668	## Host module elements
4669	
4670	`#[whisker::module_element]` creates another element builder with the common
4671	surface above plus its declared properties and `on_<event>` setters. Its schema
4672	also declares whether it accepts element or text children, whether intrinsic
4673	measurement is needed, whether resolved text style is delivered, and which
4674	imperative commands the mounted `ElementRef` may invoke.
4675	
4676	Built-ins and external module elements are equal at the runtime boundary: both
4677	resolve a registered element identity and produce the same scene/frame
4678	operations. The Host implementation decides which native object, DOM node, or
4679	Desktop renderer object represents that identity.
4680	
4681	## Refs and commands
4682	
4683	Bind with `element_ref`, not a special `ref` keyword:
4684	
4685	```rust
4686	let card = ElementRef::new();
4687	
4688	render! {
4689	    View(element_ref: card) {
4690	        Text(value: "Measured later")
4691	    }
4692	}
4693	```
4694	
4695	Built-in typed wrappers such as `ScrollViewHandle`, `TextHandle`, and
4696	`ListHandle` provide their supported commands. Module-specific wrappers should
4697	hide string command names from application code. See [Refs](/docs/refs.md).
4698	
4699	# API Reference: Reactivity
4700	
4701	Whisker's reactivity is Solid/Leptos-shaped: **signals** hold state,
4702	**computed** values derive from them, and **effects** run side effects
4703	when their dependencies change. Reads register dependencies; writes
4704	notify subscribers. Everything here comes through the prelude.
4705	
4706	```rust
4707	use whisker::prelude::*;
4708	```
4709	
4710	## The single tracking rule
4711	
4712	Reading a signal **inside a tracking context** — an `effect`, a
4713	`computed`, or a reactive prop in `render!` — subscribes that context to
4714	the signal. Reading via `.get()` at a non-reactive call site (outside any
4715	effect/computed) just returns the current value and subscribes to
4716	nothing. This is the whole model:
4717	
4718	```rust
4719	let count = signal(0);
4720	
4721	effect(move || println!("count is {}", count.get())); // subscribes
4722	let now = count.get_untracked();                       // never subscribes
4723	```
4724	
4725	Use the `_untracked` variants when you want to read a value inside an
4726	effect without making it a dependency.
4727	
4728	## `signal`
4729	
4730	```rust
4731	let count = signal(0_i32);
4732	```
4733	
4734	`signal(initial) -> RwSignal<T>` allocates a new signal in the current
4735	[owner](#owners-advanced) and returns a single combined read/write handle
4736	— an [`RwSignal<T>`](#rwsignalt). It's `Copy`, so it moves freely into
4737	`move ||` closures. Read it with `.get()` / `.with()`, write it with
4738	`.set()` / `.update()`; there is no call sugar.
4739	
4740	`signal(initial)` is the idiomatic shorthand for
4741	[`RwSignal::new(initial)`](#rwsignalt) — the two are identical.
4742	
4743	To narrow capability before handing a signal to a child, project it:
4744	`count.read_only()` yields a `ReadSignal<T>` (display, no mutation),
4745	`count.write_only()` yields a `WriteSignal<T>` (mutate only), and
4746	`count.split()` yields both halves as a `(ReadSignal<T>, WriteSignal<T>)`
4747	pair. All three view the same underlying slot.
4748	
4749	### `ReadSignal<T>`
4750	
4751	| Method           | Signature                              | Notes                                          |
4752	| ---------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
4753	| `get`            | `(self) -> T`                          | Read + subscribe. Requires `T: Clone`.         |
4754	| `get_untracked`  | `(self) -> T`                          | Read without subscribing. Requires `T: Clone`. |
4755	| `with`           | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&T) -> R) -> R` | Borrowed read + subscribe. No `Clone` bound.   |
4756	| `with_untracked` | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&T) -> R) -> R` | Borrowed read, no subscribe.                   |
4757	
4758	Use `with` / `with_untracked` when `T` is expensive to clone or isn't
4759	`Clone`.
4760	
4761	### `WriteSignal<T>`
4762	
4763	| Method             | Signature                        | Notes                                                   |
4764	| ------------------ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
4765	| `set`              | `(self, value: T)`               | Replace the value, notify subscribers.                  |
4766	| `update`           | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&mut T))` | Mutate in place, notify subscribers.                    |
4767	| `update_untracked` | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&mut T))` | Mutate without notifying. Escape hatch — use sparingly. |
4768	
4769	```rust
4770	let set_count = count.write_only(); // or: let (_, set_count) = count.split();
4771	set_count.set(1);
4772	set_count.update(|n| *n += 1);
4773	```
4774	
4775	> Writes enqueue subscriber notifications rather than running them
4776	> synchronously, to support batched event-handler semantics. The runtime
4777	> drains them each tick; see [`flush`](#owners-advanced) for the manual
4778	> drain.
4779	
4780	## `RwSignal<T>`
4781	
4782	A combined read-write handle — equivalent to holding both a
4783	`ReadSignal<T>` and a `WriteSignal<T>` for the same node. `Copy`. This is
4784	what `signal(initial)` returns, and the type you carry around for most
4785	component-local state.
4786	
4787	```rust
4788	let count = signal(0_i32);     // idiomatic; same as RwSignal::new(0_i32)
4789	count.set(1);
4790	count.update(|n| *n += 1);
4791	let n = count.get();
4792	```
4793	
4794	| Method             | Signature                                   | Notes                                                                                           |
4795	| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
4796	| `new`              | `(initial: T) -> Self`                      | Allocate in the current owner. `signal(initial)` is the free-fn shorthand.                      |
4797	| `read_only`        | `(self) -> ReadSignal<T>`                   | Project to a read-only handle on the same value. Pass this to a child that only displays state. |
4798	| `write_only`       | `(self) -> WriteSignal<T>`                  | Project to a write-only handle on the same value. Pass this to a child that only mutates.       |
4799	| `split`            | `(self) -> (ReadSignal<T>, WriteSignal<T>)` | Split into the read and write halves at once.                                                   |
4800	| `get`              | `(self) -> T`                               | Read + subscribe. `T: Clone`.                                                                   |
4801	| `get_untracked`    | `(self) -> T`                               | Read, no subscribe. `T: Clone`.                                                                 |
4802	| `with`             | `(self, f) -> R`                            | Borrowed read + subscribe.                                                                      |
4803	| `with_untracked`   | `(self, f) -> R`                            | Borrowed read, no subscribe.                                                                    |
4804	| `set`              | `(self, value: T)`                          | Replace + notify. Panics if disposed.                                                           |
4805	| `update`           | `(self, f)`                                 | Mutate + notify. Panics if disposed.                                                            |
4806	| `update_untracked` | `(self, f)`                                 | Mutate, no notify.                                                                              |
4807	| `try_set`          | `(self, value: T) -> bool`                  | Like `set`, returns `false` if the signal was already disposed.                                 |
4808	| `try_update`       | `(self, f) -> bool`                         | Like `update`, returns `false` if disposed.                                                     |
4809	
4810	`try_set` / `try_update` exist for callers that legitimately race owner
4811	disposal (e.g. a write from an `on_cleanup` callback that may fire after
4812	the signal's owner has freed its nodes). They never panic on a disposed
4813	signal.
4814	
4815	## Arc signals — `arc_signal` & the `Arc*` family
4816	
4817	The signal handles above are **arena-owned**: their lifetime is bounded
4818	by the [owner](#owners-advanced) that allocated them, and they're freed
4819	automatically when the component unmounts. That's the right default for
4820	component-local state.
4821	
4822	The `Arc*` family is **reference-counted** instead: an Arc signal owns
4823	its value through an `Rc` and stays alive as long as any handle on it
4824	remains, regardless of owner disposal. Reach for it when a signal must
4825	**outlive its declaring scope** — process-global state stashed in a
4826	`static`/`OnceLock`, state shared across components whose lifecycles
4827	don't nest (stack-navigator routes, independently-mounted tabs, portaled
4828	modals), or `HashMap<K, ArcRwSignal<V>>` collections.
4829	
4830	```rust
4831	let count = arc_signal(0_i32);
4832	count.set(1);
4833	assert_eq!(count.get(), 1);
4834	```
4835	
4836	| Type                | Role                  | Cloneability                      |
4837	| ------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------- |
4838	| `ArcRwSignal<T>`    | Combined read/write   | `Clone` (Rc bump), **not** `Copy` |
4839	| `ArcReadSignal<T>`  | Read-only projection  | `Clone`, not `Copy`               |
4840	| `ArcWriteSignal<T>` | Write-only projection | `Clone`, not `Copy`               |
4841	
4842	`arc_signal(initial) -> ArcRwSignal<T>` is the Arc analog of
4843	[`signal`](#signal) — a single combined handle. `ArcRwSignal::new`,
4844	`read_only`, `write_only`, `split`, `get`/`get_untracked`,
4845	`with`/`with_untracked`, `set`, `update`, `update_untracked` mirror the
4846	arena types' method shape exactly — the only difference is that you clone
4847	these handles explicitly (they aren't `Copy`). Use `count.split()` for
4848	the `(ArcReadSignal<T>, ArcWriteSignal<T>)` pair.
4849	
4850	Whisker also provides `From<ArcRwSignal<T>> for RwSignal<T>` (and the
4851	read/write analogs), so a module author can stash an `ArcRwSignal` at the
4852	storage boundary and hand out a `Copy` arena handle at the API surface.
4853	
4854	## `computed`
4855	
4856	```rust
4857	let count = signal(0_i32);
4858	let doubled = computed(move || count.get() * 2);
4859	assert_eq!(doubled.get(), 0);
4860	```
4861	
4862	`computed(f) -> ReadSignal<T>` (where `T: Clone + PartialEq`) creates a
4863	derived, **memoised** value — "an effect that caches its return value".
4864	The closure re-runs when a tracked source changes, and subscribers are
4865	only notified when the recomputed value **differs** from the cached one,
4866	so a computed whose result is unchanged costs nothing downstream.
4867	
4868	The returned handle is a plain `ReadSignal<T>` — read it with
4869	`.get()` / `.with()` exactly like a primitive signal. Internally `f`
4870	runs once (untracked) to seed the cache, then once more to register its
4871	dependency graph.
4872	
4873	## `effect`
4874	
4875	```rust
4876	let count = signal(0_i32);
4877	effect(move || {
4878	    println!("count changed to {}", count.get());
4879	});
4880	```
4881	
4882	`effect(f)` registers a reactive side effect. It runs **once
4883	immediately** (recording every signal it reads as a dependency) and
4884	re-runs whenever any dependency changes. The first run is synchronous —
4885	the effect has already executed by the time `effect` returns. Later runs
4886	are scheduled and drained at flush time.
4887	
4888	## Context
4889	
4890	Pass values down the owner tree without threading props.
4891	`provide_context::<T>(value)` stores a value in the current owner;
4892	lookups walk up the owner chain to the nearest provider.
4893	
4894	| Function          | Signature                                | Notes                                                                    |
4895	| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
4896	| `provide_context` | `(value: T)`                             | Store a `T` in the current owner. Re-providing the same `T` replaces it. |
4897	| `use_context`     | `() -> Option<T>`                        | Nearest provided `T`, cloned. `T: Clone`.                                |
4898	| `with_context`    | `(f: impl FnOnce(&T) -> R) -> Option<R>` | Borrow the nearest `T` without cloning.                                  |
4899	
4900	```rust
4901	#[derive(Clone)]
4902	struct Theme { dark: bool }
4903	
4904	provide_context(Theme { dark: true });
4905	
4906	// in a descendant:
4907	let theme = use_context::<Theme>().expect("Theme provided above");
4908	```
4909	
4910	Use `with_context` when `T` is expensive to clone or you only need a
4911	borrow.
4912	
4913	## Async data — `resource`
4914	
4915	A resource runs an async fetcher and exposes its loading / ready / error
4916	state through a `Copy` handle. See [Tasks & Threading](/docs/tasks.md) for
4917	`spawn_local` and `run_blocking`, which resources build on.
4918	
4919	```rust
4920	let stories = resource(|| async {
4921	    run_blocking(|| {
4922	        ureq::get("https://example.com/feed.json")
4923	            .call()
4924	            .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
4925	            .into_string()
4926	            .map_err(|e| e.to_string())
4927	    })
4928	    .await
4929	    .and_then(|body| parse(&body))
4930	});
4931	```
4932	
4933	| Function        | Signature                  | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                              |
4934	| --------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
4935	| `resource`      | `(fetcher) -> Resource<T>` | Spawns the fetcher on the task pool. Returns immediately in `Loading`. **Reactive:** the fetcher runs in an effect, so signals it reads are tracked and it **re-fetches when any of them change**. |
4936	| `resource_sync` | `(fetcher) -> Resource<T>` | Runs the fetcher inline (no worker thread). Resolves to `Ready`/`Error` immediately, never `Loading`. **One-shot / untracked** — does not subscribe to signals it reads, so it never re-fetches.   |
4937	
4938	The `fetcher` returns `Result<T, String>` — by convention you stringify
4939	upstream errors with `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())`.
4940	
4941	### Reactive re-fetching
4942	
4943	`resource` takes a single fetcher closure (there is no separate `source`
4944	argument). The closure runs inside an effect, so any signal read while it
4945	runs — including reads **inside the async block** — becomes a dependency:
4946	
4947	```rust
4948	let query = signal(String::new());
4949	let results = resource(move || async move {
4950	    let q = query.get();   // tracked → changing `query` re-fetches
4951	    run_blocking(move || api::search(&q)).await.map_err(|e| e.to_string())
4952	});
4953	```
4954	
4955	The semantics:
4956	
4957	- **Re-fetch on change** — when a tracked signal changes the fetcher runs
4958	  again with the new value.
4959	- **Returns to `Loading`** — each re-fetch resets the resource to
4960	  `Loading` until the new result lands.
4961	- **Latest-wins generation guard** — if a tracked signal changes again
4962	  before an in-flight fetch resolves, the stale result is discarded; only
4963	  the most recent run commits.
4964	
4965	Put a signal in the fetcher when it decides _what to fetch_. If a signal
4966	only _transforms already-fetched data_, wrap the resource in a `computed`
4967	instead of re-fetching. See
4968	[Async & Data Loading](/docs/async-and-data.md) for the worked pattern.
4969	
4970	### `Resource<T>`
4971	
4972	`Copy`. Requires `T: Clone`.
4973	
4974	| Method       | Signature                                     | Notes                                               |
4975	| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
4976	| `get`        | `(&self) -> Option<T>`                        | `Some(value)` when ready, else `None`.              |
4977	| `loading`    | `(&self) -> bool`                             | `true` while the fetch is in flight.                |
4978	| `error`      | `(&self) -> Option<String>`                   | `Some(message)` if the fetch failed.                |
4979	| `state`      | `(&self) -> ResourceState<T>`                 | The full state (reactive read).                     |
4980	| `from_state` | `(state: RwSignal<ResourceState<T>>) -> Self` | Build a synthetic resource from an existing signal. |
4981	
4982	All accessors read the underlying signal reactively — calling them inside
4983	a `render!` prop or an effect re-renders on state transitions.
4984	
4985	### `ResourceState<T>`
4986	
4987	```rust
4988	pub enum ResourceState<T> {
4989	    Loading,
4990	    Ready(T),
4991	    Error(String),
4992	}
4993	```
4994	
4995	| Method       | Returns | True when           |
4996	| ------------ | ------- | ------------------- |
4997	| `is_loading` | `bool`  | state is `Loading`  |
4998	| `is_ready`   | `bool`  | state is `Ready(_)` |
4999	| `is_error`   | `bool`  | state is `Error(_)` |
5000	
5001	## `StoredValue<T>`
5002	
5003	`Copy` owner-bound storage that does **not** participate in reactivity —
5004	reads don't subscribe and writes don't notify. It's the scoped
5005	equivalent of `Rc<RefCell<...>>`: share non-reactive state across
5006	closures in a component and have it freed automatically on unmount.
5007	
5008	| Method   | Signature                                  | Notes                            |
5009	| -------- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
5010	| `new`    | `(initial: T) -> Self`                     | Allocate in the current owner.   |
5011	| `get`    | `(self) -> T`                              | Read (no subscribe). `T: Clone`. |
5012	| `with`   | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&T) -> R) -> R`     | Borrowed read.                   |
5013	| `update` | `(self, f: impl FnOnce(&mut T) -> R) -> R` | Borrowed mutation (no notify).   |
5014	| `set`    | `(self, value: T)`                         | Replace the value.               |
5015	
5016	## The Signal prop type
5017	
5018	> Reachable at `/docs/reactivity-api#the-signal-prop-type`.
5019	
5020	`Signal<T>` is the **prop value type** used by `#[component]`,
5021	built-in elements, and `#[whisker::module_element]` builders. It encodes
5022	"this prop accepts either a plain value **or** a reactive signal":
5023	
5024	```rust
5025	pub enum Signal<T> {
5026	    Static(T),              // plain value — set once
5027	    Dynamic(ReadSignal<T>), // reactive handle — tracked, updates live
5028	}
5029	```
5030	
5031	A builder method takes `impl Into<Signal<T>>`, so the call-site
5032	conversion is implicit. Passing a `T` yields `Static`; passing a
5033	`ReadSignal`, `RwSignal`, or the `ReadSignal` returned by
5034	[`computed`](#computed) yields `Dynamic`. A `&str` literal converts to
5035	`Signal::Static(String)`.
5036	
5037	| `From` impl                       | Produces                              |
5038	| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
5039	| `From<T>`                         | `Signal::Static(value)`               |
5040	| `From<ReadSignal<T>>`             | `Signal::Dynamic`                     |
5041	| `From<RwSignal<T>>`               | `Signal::Dynamic` (via `read_only()`) |
5042	| `From<&str>` for `Signal<String>` | `Signal::Static(String)`              |
5043	
5044	Read a `Signal<T>` prop with `.get()`:
5045	
5046	- `Static` returns a clone of the held value — no reactivity.
5047	- `Dynamic` forwards to `ReadSignal::get`, which **subscribes** the
5048	  current tracking context.
5049	
5050	```rust
5051	#[component]
5052	fn badge(label: Signal<String>) -> Element {
5053	    let style = computed(move || format!("content: {}", label.get()));
5054	    render! { View(style: style) { Text(value: label) } }
5055	}
5056	
5057	// static prop:
5058	render! { Badge(label: "items") }
5059	// reactive prop:
5060	render! { Badge(label: my_signal) }
5061	```
5062	
5063	This is exactly the [static-vs-dynamic distinction](/docs/macros.md) the
5064	`render!` macro surfaces: pass a signal handle for reactivity, or
5065	pre-read it with `signal.get()` to capture a one-shot static snapshot.
5066	
5067	## Owners (advanced)
5068	
5069	> Framework-extension surface. Application code almost never touches
5070	> these directly — `#[component]`, `provide_context`, `on_cleanup`, and
5071	> friends set up and tear down owners for you. Reach here when authoring
5072	> custom control flow, a router, or a custom renderer. Available via
5073	> `whisker::runtime::owner` / `whisker::owner`.
5074	
5075	An `Owner` is a reactive **scope**: the lifetime unit that ties together
5076	signals, effects, computeds, element handles, and cleanup callbacks.
5077	Disposing an owner cascades into its children, frees every node it
5078	allocated, releases its element handles, and runs its cleanup callbacks
5079	in LIFO order.
5080	
5081	| Method       | Signature                            | Notes                                                                               |
5082	| ------------ | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
5083	| `Owner::new` | `(parent: Option<Owner>) -> Owner`   | `None` ⇒ child of the current owner. Inherits the parent's paused flag.             |
5084	| `with`       | `(self, f: impl FnOnce() -> R) -> R` | Run `f` with `self` as the current scope; primitives allocated inside belong to it. |
5085	| `dispose`    | `(self)`                             | Tear down the scope and all descendants. Idempotent.                                |
5086	| `pause`      | `(self)`                             | Freeze the subtree — scheduled effects defer instead of running.                    |
5087	| `resume`     | `(self)`                             | Unfreeze and re-queue deferred effects.                                             |
5088	| `is_paused`  | `(self) -> bool`                     | Mainly for tests.                                                                   |
5089	
5090	`pause` / `resume` back off-screen-but-mounted UI (e.g. back-stack
5091	routes) — state survives but no CPU is spent on signal-driven re-renders
5092	behind the top route.
5093	
5094	### Lifecycle free functions
5095	
5096	| Function     | Signature                      | Notes                                                                                                         |
5097	| ------------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
5098	| `on_mount`   | `(f: impl FnOnce() + 'static)` | Fires once after the component's view is appended to the tree.                                                |
5099	| `on_cleanup` | `(f: impl FnOnce() + 'static)` | Runs when the current owner is disposed. Accumulates LIFO.                                                    |
5100	| `flush`      | `()`                           | Drain the pending queue, re-running scheduled effects/computeds now. No-op if a flush is already in progress. |
5101	
5102	`on_mount` is the right place for post-mount measurement or kicking off
5103	background work; `on_cleanup` for releasing resources. `flush` is rarely
5104	needed in app code — the runtime drains every tick — but is essential in
5105	tests and custom drivers to force pending effects to run.
5106

5111	functions you call inside [`render!`](/docs/macros.md) like any other
